
=================================================================
#78 Pyongyang I  (661 December)
Arc: The Final Stand · place: pyongyang · tone: grim war epic
Logline: A red gate on a grey ridge. There is only one gate anyone remembers.
=================================================================
[0] ¶ Pyongyang has never fallen. Every child in the city will tell you so, usually twice.
[1] ¶ Red Sun's capital sits on its ridge: a red two-storey gate, grey stone, and clouds that always look about to pick a side. The last emperor tried these walls. So did the one before him. The walls are still here.
[2] [MAP 661: A fleet up the river, an army at the Amnok, and a winter about to pick a side.]
[3] ── SCENE: The Wall ──
[4] ¶ Up on the wall, Gesomun's second son is explaining this to a sentry who did not ask.
[5] [CARD Yeon Namgun: Gesomun’s second son. Loud, loyal, and he believes everything he’s told twice.]
[6] Yeon Namgun: Pyongyang does not fall. / Not since the Holy King strung his bow. Seven hundred years.
[7] Yeon Namsan: You said that yesterday.
[8] Yeon Namgun: It was true yesterday too.
[9] ¶ Their father walks the wall behind them with a scout’s report in his fist. A Mohe man walks one step behind him, as he has for twenty-seven years. Nobody introduces Gulgul. Nobody ever has.
[10] Yeon Gesomun: Four beasts, it says. The emperor sends animals now. / One of them brought his sons. All thirteen of them.
[11] Yeon Namgun: Thirteen? He brought children to a war?
[12] Yeon Gesomun: Not children. Grown men. / They came to watch their father work.
[13] ¶ He says it the way other men mention rain. Then he goes down the stairs to send his eldest north, to hold the river.
[14] ── SCENE: Luoyang ──
[15] ¶ In Luoyang the Third Emperor announces that he will lead the next army himself. The Empress sends up a memorial the same night.
[16] Wu Zetian: Your father went in person, Majesty. / Ask the six horses at Zhaoling how that went.
[17] The Third Emperor: …We will send someone.
[18] ── SCENE: The Taedong ──
[19] ¶ The someone is the Red Fowl, the old steppe horseman who took Sabi. He comes up the Taedong in the eighth month and takes the river forts one by one. Then he sits down in front of Pyongyang to wait for winter to soften it. Winter has never been on anybody’s side but Goguryeo’s.
[20] ── SCENE: The Frozen River ──
[21] ¶ Namseng holds the Amnok. He is twenty-seven, the heir, and he has read every record of every crossing.
[22] ¶ His orders are simple. Tens of thousands of picked men, one river, nobody across. On the far bank waits the White Dragon, the old emperor’s Turkish general. He once asked to be buried alive beside his master. They told him no. He has been looking for a useful place to die ever since.
[23] ¶ Then the ninth month turns cold. Not autumn cold. Wrong cold.
[24] officer: Commander. The shallows are white. / …The middle’s going too.
[25] Yeon Namseng: The river has never frozen hard in the ninth month. / Not in any record.
[26] officer: Sir. The river hasn’t read the records.
[27] ¶ At dawn the drums start on the far bank. The White Dragon does not build a bridge. He walks out onto the ice himself, leading his horse, and stamps twice.
[28] ¶ It holds. His army follows him across a river that is no longer there, drumming as it comes. The first Goguryeo arrows skitter off the ice. The second volley never comes. Men who were told to guard water do not know how to guard a floor.
[29] Yeon Namseng: Hold the bank! Hold— the bank is—
[30] ¶ There is no bank. There is only ice, and then there is everywhere. Thirty thousand men die defending a line that has gone white. Namseng gets away with his life and very little else.
[31] ── SCENE: The Gate ──
[32] ¶ He comes home through the fortress gate at dusk, on a borrowed horse. His father is waiting under the red gate. Gulgul holds the lamp.
[33] Yeon Gesomun: One river, Namseng. I gave you one river. / Don’t tell me you didn’t know it would freeze. It freezes every year.
[34] Yeon Namseng: Not in the ninth month, Father. There is no precedent—
[35] Yeon Gesomun: Precedent! The river can’t read, you idiot.
[36] Yeon Namgun: Father, he brought the men home. Half of them—
[37] Yeon Gesomun: Half. He left with all of them.
[38] ¶ Nobody speaks. Namseng waits for the blow. He has been waiting for one since he was eleven, at the Liao, when an emperor’s men gave it to him instead.
[39] ¶ It does not come. Gesomun lays a hand on the iron studs of the gate, the way you would test a horse’s leg.
[40] Yeon Gesomun: Listen. Walls don’t fall. Nobody’s ever knocked these down. / Gates get opened. From the inside. / This one’s yours now. Remember which side of it you’re standing on.
[41] Yeon Namseng: …Yes, Father.
[42] ¶ Remember this gate. All three of his sons will.
[43] ── SCENE: The Campfires ──
[44] ¶ The Red Fowl’s army freezes in the snow outside the walls. Every night Gesomun counts its campfires from the parapet. Every night there are fewer.
[45] Yeon Gesomun: They’re eating the horses. Fires go down when the horses run out. / Keep counting, Gulgul. The night they stop going down, somebody’s feeding them.
[46] Gulgul: …Yes, sir.
[47] ── SCENE: Surabol ──
[48] ¶ In the twelfth month a letter comes down from the north. The Red Fowl is out of rice. Munmu reads it to his generals. Everyone in the room knows that road in winter. Nobody offers.
[49] King Munmu: If they starve out there, the emperor will remember who let them. / And everything my father was promised starves with them.
[50] ¶ Silence. Then Kim Yushin, who is sixty-six, gets up.
[51] King Munmu: Uncle. Not you. Send someone younger.
[52] Kim Yushin: The younger ones don’t know the road, Majesty. Hanseul and I do. / Load the carts.
[53] [MAP 662: Rice for the Red Fowl, through enemy country, in the dead of winter, driven by the oldest general in Silla.]
[54] ¶ **The White Tiger has thirteen sons. Yeon Gesomun can count to thirteen…!**

=================================================================
#79 Snake River  (662 February)
Arc: The Final Stand · place: sasu · tone: grim war epic
Logline: The White Tiger still believes rivers are roads. Yeon Gesomun has been waiting for a man who thinks that.
=================================================================
[0] ¶ The White Tiger drives his host into the Snake River. They still believe rivers are roads. Yeon Gesomun has been waiting for a man who thinks that. Old men in the north remember another river that ate an army. The Snake is younger. It's hungrier. And it has Yeon's teeth.
[1] [PLACE sasu: Shallow, slow, and patient with men who think rivers are roads.]
[2] [MAP 662: The White Tiger thought the river was a road. Yeon is standing in the middle of it.]
[3] ── SCENE: The Ford ──
[4] ¶ Here is the plan, such as it is. The Tiger is marching to join the Red Fowl outside Pyongyang. If he gets there, the city is in a ring.
[5] [CARD White Tiger: The White Tiger. A Tang general who brought all his sons to war, to show them how it’s done.]
[6] ¶ Gesomun lets him get halfway. The Snake has gravel at the edges and mud in the middle, and Gesomun knows which is which.
[7] Yeon Gesomun: He thinks it’s a road. Let him walk on it. / When the middle horses sink — both banks. All at once.
[8] ¶ The middle horses sink. Both banks open up at once.
[9] ── SCENE: Thirteen Sons ──
[10] ¶ The river does not take them in a heap. Yeon counts. Chang’an’s clerks will later write _thirteen sons_ as if a number were a grave. It is a morning. The water is February-cold.
[11] ¶ The thirteenth and the twelfth come together at the first bend — brothers who still share a horse’s width. Yeon meets them in the shallows where the current lies. One stroke. Two bodies. The horse walks on a few steps with no one left to tell it to stop.
[12] Yeon Gesomun: Thirteen. / Twelve.
[13] ¶ The eleventh tries the reeds. Reeds keep a secret until a man breathes too loud. Yeon does not spend a speech on a boy hiding in grass.
[14] Yeon Gesomun: Eleven.
[15] ¶ The tenth and the ninth turn back toward their father. That is the expensive choice. They die reaching for a sleeve that is still too far upriver.
[16] Yeon Gesomun: Ten. / Nine.
[17] ¶ The eighth is the archer. He puts three shafts into the rim of Yeon’s shield and the fourth into his horse’s neck. The horse goes down, and Yeon goes into the water with it.
[18] ── SCENE: Yumla Defied ──
[19] ¶ In the worst hour of it — arrows spent, horse down, a Tang blade a finger from his throat — the air thins the way Tamla stories promised. The river stops moving. **Kangrim** and **Haewonmek** are standing on it, a ledger half-open between them.
[20] Kangrim: Yeon Gesomun. / Your page is… persuasive today.
[21] Kangrim: Commander. If you walk away now — / are you choosing Goguryeo, or choosing not to be finished by anyone else’s schedule?
[22] Haewonmek: Any last words? / Say them now. The blade is already practicing your name.
[23] Yeon Gesomun: Kangrim. Haewonmek. / Both. / And neither is your business until I am done.
[24] Yeon Gesomun: Not today. / I still have sons to disappoint.
[25] ¶ Then he turns his back on them. He takes hold of his own body the way you take a coat off a peg, and puts it back on. The river starts moving again.
[26] ¶ He stands up on will alone. The blade misses. He breaks the spearman’s wrist before the man has finished the thrust. Behind him, the two reapers close the ledger with something like respect.
[27] Kangrim: Hah. / Keep the country a little longer, then. / I hate refiling — and Your Majesty hates wasted parchment.
[28] Haewonmek: Next time we bring a longer chain. / Or a taller boss.
[29] ¶ The archer is still nocking his fifth arrow. He does not finish it. Afterward Yeon takes the bow out of the water and breaks it across his knee.
[30] Yeon Gesomun: Eight. The bow ends here.
[31] ¶ The seventh almost makes the far bank. Yeon’s throw finds him between the shoulder-blades, and the current carries him the rest of the way.
[32] the seventh: Baekju… / Home…
[33] Yeon Gesomun: Seven. Home is not that bank.
[34] ¶ Three at once in a knot of horses: the sixth, the fifth, the fourth. They shout one father’s name in three pitches.
[35] Yeon Gesomun: Six. Five. Four. / Some days you count in threes.
[36] ¶ The third is old enough to bargain. He offers the banner, the southern levy, a road south, if the Mangniji will count him as a messenger instead of a son.
[37] the third: Let me go as a messenger. / Among the thirteen I am the only one who opened his mouth.
[38] Yeon Gesomun: You did not come as a messenger. / That is why you are three.
[39] ¶ The second is younger. He does not speak. Yeon does not ask him to.
[40] Yeon Gesomun: Two.
[41] ¶ The first — the eldest — holds the White Tiger banner with both hands so the silk will not touch the water. He lasts longer than the others because he has decided to be a flagpole. Yeon cuts the pole. The cloth goes under. The boy goes with it, still holding on, which is how eldest sons are trained.
[42] Yeon Gesomun: One. / Now the tiger.
[43] ── SCENE: The White Tiger ──
[44] ¶ Then only the tiger is left. He stands where his boys could still see him, if any of them still had eyes. Someone shouts to break east, toward any camp that is not this one.
[45] aide: Commander! Toward You Boying’s camp— / Live, and leave the account!
[46] White Tiger: I have eaten too much favour under two emperors. / I will not go home while this kingdom still stands. / The southern boys I brought are already dead — / what would this one body do, alive?
[47] ¶ He does not run. The arrows make a hedgehog of him. Yeon walks the last three steps through the water and finishes what the shafts began.
[48] Yeon Gesomun: White Tiger. / Titles drown too.
[49] Yeon Gesomun: Still haven’t come to your senses, you bastards?! / I am… none other than… Yeon Gesomun!!
[50] ── SCENE: The Rice Road ──
[51] ¶ In the second month a train of carts comes up out of the south through snow to the axles. **Kim Yushin** is sixty-seven, and he has walked half the road beside his white horse so that Hanseul can carry a sack of rice instead of him.
[52] ¶ The Tang camp outside Pyongyang has been eating its horses. Men sit hugging their knees in the snow and look at the carts as if they might be another rumour.
[53] ¶ On Pyongyang’s wall that night, Gulgul counts the Tang fires twice. They have stopped going down.
[54] Yeon Gesomun: Somebody’s feeding them. / …Find out who. Then follow him home.
[55] Red Fowl: Silla is late. / …Unload it. All of it. Then we go home.
[56] Kim Yushin: We came through snow to the horse’s chest, General. / You may eat it slowly.
[57] ¶ The Red Fowl takes the rice, breaks camp within the week, and sails. The road back is Yushin’s problem. Goguryeo’s horsemen follow the empty carts all the way to the Imjin, and the white horse carries him across it.
[58] ── SCENE: The Far West ──
[59] ¶ A thousand miles the other way, the courier finds Xue Rengui. You may remember him: the farmer in the white coat who left his ancestors unburied to answer a muster. He has just ended a war in the far west with three arrows. Now he is given the dead man’s title, White Tiger II. And the bill.
[60] Xue Rengui: White Tiger… I will take the name. / The dead man’s account is paid by the living.
[61] ¶ The fangtian ji goes east again. Men who never learned his birth name learn the white coat and the crescent blade — and begin, quietly, to fear the second tiger more than the first.
[62] ¶ **And on an island far to the south, someone is asking: whose side are we on now?**

=================================================================
#80 Tamla Surrenders  (662 February)
Arc: The Final Stand · place: mugun · tone: island coda
Logline: Two envoys, one fire, and an island king who won’t pick only one side.
=================================================================
[0] ¶ “Whose side are we on now?” On Tamla, the one who asks is usually holding a fish.
[1] [MAP 662: An island off the bottom of the map, with two kingdoms’ boats in its harbour.]
[2] ¶ This time it is a diver, still wet from the morning, with an octopus in one fist. She asks it in the king’s hall, loudly, because the king’s hall is also where the island dries its nets.
[3] ¶ Yuri Dora does not answer at once. He never answers anything at once. He has a fire, two cups, and two envoys who will not sit down.
[4] ¶ One came down from the last Baekje hill fort. The other came from Silla, with a Tang officer behind him like a second shadow.
[5] ── SCENE: Two Envoys ──
[6] Baekje envoy: Seven hundred years, my lord. Your fathers carried our ranks. / Boksin asks for boats. Grain. Any man who can hold an oar.
[7] Silla envoy: The Snake River went badly for the Tang, my lord. It will not go badly twice. / My king asks for nothing but your name on a list.
[8] Yuri Dora: Only my name. You hear that? Only a name. / Names are the dearest thing on this island. We have so few.
[9] Tang officer: The emperor’s fleet sails past this island on its way to everywhere, my lord. / It could stop.
[10] Yuri Dora: Then it can stop for oranges. Everyone does.
[11] The Divers: Feed them first, my lord. Nobody decides anything hungry.
[12] ¶ So they eat. Raw octopus, barley, a bowl of something orange. The Baekje envoy eats like a man who has not seen a full bowl since Sabi. The Silla envoy eats like a man being watched, which he is.
[13] ── SCENE: The Turtle ──
[14] ¶ Then the Baekje envoy plays the only card he brought.
[15] Baekje envoy: My lord. The general they called Hundred-Victories lived here five years. / He died at the Yellow Mountain, for Baekje. Fighting these men’s army. / Will you bow to the side that killed him?
[16] ¶ The hall goes quiet. Even the divers stop chewing. Every one of them remembers the Turtle.
[17] ¶ Yuri Dora turns his cup in his hands for a long time.
[18] Yuri Dora: The first night, he asked me how many days. Not hello. How many days. / Five years. He never once sat down by this fire.
[19] ¶ He fills the second cup anyway and sets it by the door, where a man used to stand.
[20] Baekje envoy: Then you owe him—
[21] Yuri Dora: I told him one thing when he left. Do not forget people. / I didn’t say, don’t forget kings. Kings he remembered fine. Look where it got him.
[22] ¶ He points his cup at the door. Outside, on the black rock by the eastern shore, a handful of children are drilling in fives, badly, out of step. Nobody taught them. They learned it by standing behind a man who never turned round.
[23] Yuri Dora: Those are my people. That’s who I’m not forgetting.
[24] ── SCENE: Two Boats ──
[25] ¶ So the king of Tamla makes his choice the way the island does everything: sideways.
[26] Yuri Dora: Get two boats ready. / One goes to Silla with my name for their list. Make them spell it right. / The other takes him back up to his hill fort. Barley, oranges, whatever the divers can spare.
[27] Silla envoy: My lord— you cannot bow to both.
[28] Yuri Dora: Watch me. I’m an island. I don’t have a side. I have a harbour. / And a story isn’t begun with its ending already fixed.
[29] The Divers: …So whose side are we on?
[30] Yuri Dora: Ours. Eat your octopus.
[31] ¶ The two boats leave on the same tide, one east, one north. From the black rock the children wave at both. Nobody has told them which one to wave at.
[32] ¶ In the emperor’s city, a clerk writes the visit down. He has never seen the island. It shows.
[33] ❝QUOTE (Xin Tangshu (新唐書) bk. 220, Eastern Barbarians — Danluo (儋羅, Tamla), Longshuo era (661–663)): Early in Longshuo there was a land called Danluo, whose king, Yuri Dora, sent envoys to court. It lies on an island south of Silla's Muju. Its ways are plain and rough: they wear the hides of great pigs, live in leather huts in summer and in pit-houses in winter. … At first it was attached to Baekje. … Later it attached itself to Silla.❞
[34] ¶ **Baekje refuses to stay dead. And in Surabol, a great lord feels a fever coming on…!**

=================================================================
#81 Rebellion  (662 August)
Arc: The Final Stand · place: surabol · tone: court purge drama
Logline: Nineteen generals are named for the campaign. Two of them call in sick, and are seen at a gyuku match.
=================================================================
[0] ¶ Kim Jinju has a fever. Half of Surabol has watched it play gyuku.
[1] ── SCENE: Naesaji ──
[2] ¶ Two summers after Sabi, Baekje is supposed to be finished. Baekje has not been informed. Its leftovers hold a hill fort east of the old capital. They collect grain. They hang collaborators. They send boys to watch the Silla roads.
[3] [MAP 662: ]
[4] ¶ Munmu names nineteen generals for it. One of them is Kim Jinju. He is True Bone, from a good family. He led men at the Yellow Mountain. He has a son in the emperor's guard.
[5] ── SCENE: Sick Leave ──
[6] ¶ Jinju sends word that he is ill. So does his friend **Jinheum**. Neither of them is ill. They stay home through the whole campaign, eat well, and receive visitors.
[7] Kim Jinju: Nineteen generals for one hill fort. They don’t need a twentieth. / Besides. The war’s over. Somebody should say so.
[8] ¶ The gyuku field is full that week. Jinju plays well for a sick man. Between rounds, Jinheum leans on the rail beside him.
[9] Jinheum: The king’s man is in the stands. Third row. He hasn’t watched the ball once.
[10] Kim Jinju: Let him count. My son stands at the emperor’s door. / Munmu won’t touch a house with a boy in Chang’an. He needs the emperor too much.
[11] ¶ It is a good argument. It is the argument every lord in the city would make. Munmu has been king for one year, and nobody knows yet what he is.
[12] ── SCENE: The Moon Palace ──
[13] ¶ Naesaji falls without him. Kim Heumsun takes it in a fortnight and reports it to the king in two lines, and then, because he is honest and it is his duty, he reports who was missing.
[14] ¶ Before he sends for them, Munmu asks his uncle one question.
[15] King Munmu: Uncle. If I spare them?
[16] Kim Yushin: Then next year you name nineteen generals, Majesty, and seventeen come.
[17] King Munmu: And when Jinju’s son hears of it in Chang’an?
[18] Kim Yushin: He’ll hear either way. Better he hears you meant it.
[19] King Munmu: Ill. / The whole campaign. Both of them. And well enough for gyuku.
[20] Kim Jinju: Majesty, the fever came and went. A man cannot choose his days—
[21] King Munmu: My father never had a day off from this war. My sister didn’t get to choose hers. / Take them out.
[22] Kim Jinju: Majesty— my son. He’s in the emperor’s guard. / Someone has to write to him—
[23] King Munmu: I’ll write to him myself.
[24] ¶ Jinju and Jinheum are beheaded, and their households with them, down to the cousins. It is the first time Munmu kills his own nobility. After it, nobody in Surabol mistakes the new king for a soft one.
[25] ¶ He writes the letter that night. It is short. He does not ask a secretary to do it.
[26] ── SCENE: Chang’an ──
[27] ¶ **Kim Punghun** is in Chang’an when the letter comes, in the emperor’s guard, where vassal houses keep their sons. He reads it twice. He hears the rest from a Tang officer who is sorry for him, which is worse. He asks for leave to go home for the mourning and is told, kindly, that he has no home to go to.
[28] Kim Punghun: …Then I will wait. / The emperor’s ships go east sooner or later. I can wait for a ship.
[29] ¶ Remember the boy. The emperor’s ships do go east, eventually.
[30] ¶ **Meanwhile at Juryu, the general who crowned Baekje’s king has taken to his bed. He would love a visit…!**

=================================================================
#82 Betrayal  (663 June)
Arc: The Final Stand · place: juryu · tone: resistance tragedy
Logline: The general who crowned Baekje’s king is sick in bed and asking for a visit. The king remembers another supper.
=================================================================
[0] ¶ Boksin is sick. It is the healthiest he has looked in years.
[1] ¶ For nine days he has not left his bed at Juryu. Every morning he sends the same message up the hill. The king should come. He has something to say that cannot be said in a hall.
[2] [MAP 663: ]
[3] ── SCENE: The King’s Room ──
[4] ¶ King Pung reads the message nine times. Then he sends for **Heukchi Sangji**, who took back two hundred fortresses for Boksin in a single season and has never once made a speech about it.
[5] Prince Pung: He is your general, Sangji. Should I go?
[6] Heukchi Sangji: He’s your general, Majesty. Not mine.
[7] Prince Pung: …Do you know what happened to the monk?
[8] Heukchi Sangji: He went on a retreat, Majesty. That’s what we were told.
[9] Prince Pung: That is what I was told too. The morning after a supper.
[10] ¶ He was new then, and did not know much. He knew what a supper was, though.
[11] ▼ FLASHBACK 661 the monk’s supper
    [11.0] ¶ Before Boksin and the king, there were Boksin and the monk. Dochim raised the first banner with him, the autumn Sabi fell. He put down his begging bowl for a spear. He named himself General of the Spirit Army. For a year the two held the west between them. The enemy garrison couldn't even go out for water.
    [11.1] ❝QUOTE (Dhammapada (法句經) ch. 18, Sword and Rod (刀杖品), tr. Weiqinan & Zhu Jiangyan · T04n0210, p. 565b · Pali: Dhammapada 129, Daṇḍavagga) [Dochim]: All fear death; there is none who does not dread the pain of the rod. Take yourself as the measure: do not kill, do not strike.❞
    [11.2] ¶ Then a Tang envoy came to the walls with a letter, and Dochim sent him back with it unread and a message that the General of the Spirit Army did not receive men of so small a rank. It was a good line. Boksin heard it and understood that the monk had begun to think of himself as the one in charge.
    [11.3] Dochim: The Buddha gave me this army, Boksin. You only fed it. / Feed it well. It is going to Sabi.
    [11.4] Gwishil Boksin: Of course, General. Whatever the Spirit Army needs. / Supper tonight, then. Just the two of us. We’ll talk about Sabi.
    [11.5] ¶ Dochim comes to supper. He does not leave it. By morning his men have been folded into Boksin’s army without a vote, and Prince Pung, newly crowned and still learning the names, is told that the monk has gone on a long retreat.
    [11.6] Prince Pung: A retreat. In the middle of a war. / …I see. And who commands his men now?
    [11.7] Gwishil Boksin: I do, Majesty. So that Your Majesty need never worry about it.
[11] ▲ end flashback
[12] ¶ Pung remembers the answer. He has had two years to think about it.
[13] ── SCENE: The Sickbed ──
[14] ¶ Sangji goes down the hill instead. He finds Boksin propped on cushions, eating well. There is a screen behind the bed. Under the screen, Sangji counts four pairs of boots.
[15] Gwishil Boksin: Sangji. Sit. Is His Majesty coming?
[16] Heukchi Sangji: At dusk, General.
[17] Gwishil Boksin: You know, it’s I who raised this country. Twice. / And it’s he who wears the crown.
[18] Heukchi Sangji: Four pairs of boots under that screen, General.
[19] Gwishil Boksin: Guests. A sick man gets lonely. / …And he’ll want to move the court again. You know he will.
[20] ¶ Sangji looks at the boots a while longer. Then he goes back up the hill. He is up there a long time.
[21] ── SCENE: Dusk ──
[22] ¶ The king comes at dusk, as promised. He brings the Yamato guard, which was not promised.
[23] Prince Pung: General. You look terribly well.
[24] Gwishil Boksin: Majesty. Forgive me for not rising.
[25] Prince Pung: I hear you have risen twice already. That is plenty.
[26] ¶ Boksin looks past the king, at Sangji. Sangji is looking at the screen.
[27] ¶ The guards pull the screen down. The four guests are holding knives, which is an odd thing to bring to a sickroom.
[28] ¶ That night Pung has the general who crowned him bound with a leather thong through the palms. He asks the room whether a man like that should be cut down. The room says yes. A courtier named Jipdeuk says it first and loudest. Boksin spits at him.
[29] ❝QUOTE (Nihon Shoki (日本書紀) bk. 27, Tenji 2 (663), sixth month): Boksin at once spat at Jipdeuk and said: “Rotten dog, idiot slave!” The king ordered his strong men to behead him, and had the head pickled.❞
[30] ¶ Two generals stand at the back while the head is salted. **Heukchi Sangji**, who took two hundred fortresses back for Boksin in a single season, watches the king’s hands. **Satek Sangya** watches the jar.
[31] Heukchi Sangji: The man who crowned him. In a jar. / …What do you think he does with the ones who didn’t?
[32] Satek Sangya: Same thing. Less salt.
[33] ¶ Neither of them says what the whole hill is thinking. Boksin was the only general they had who ever won anything.
[34] ¶ **Four banners. One river mouth. The West, Samhan and the East meet on a single tide…!**

=================================================================
#83 White River  (663 August)
Arc: The Final Stand · place: baekgang · tone: grim war epic — naval
Logline: For the first time, the West, Samhan and the East meet in one mouth of water. The tide is nobody’s friend.
=================================================================
[0] ¶ Four banners come to one river mouth. Only the tide has been here before.
[1] ¶ The White River empties into the western sea through sandbars that move like rumours. Whoever holds its mouth holds what is left of Baekje.
[2] [MAP 663: ]
[3] ── SCENE: Four Banners ──
[4] ¶ The Tang come by sea. The Black Tortoise has held the old capital for two winters with too few men. The emperor offered to bring him home. He wrote back that he’d rather not. So the emperor sent more.
[5] ¶ Silla comes by land. King Munmu rides out with Kim Yushin and every general he has. Yushin is sixty-eight and still sits a horse as if the horse had asked him to.
[6] ¶ Baekje is what is left of it: a hill fort called Juryu, a king raised overseas, and no Boksin.
[7] ¶ So the East sends sails. Hundreds of them, packed too tight to row. Takutsu is among the captains. He brought Pung home two years ago. Last winter he told him not to move the court down to the plain. He was right, and was thanked for it the way men usually are.
[8] ── SCENE: The King Leaves ──
[9] ¶ On the thirteenth day of the eighth month, with the Silla army already on the road to Juryu, the king of Baekje announces that he will leave it.
[10] Prince Pung: Yamato’s relief general is crossing the sea with ten thousand men and more. / Generals, make ready for him. / I shall go down to the river mouth myself, and receive them there with a feast.
[11] 🙇: Majesty. And Juryu?
[12] Prince Pung: Juryu has walls.
[13] 🙇: …It had a general, too.
[14] ── SCENE: The Throat of the River ──
[15] ¶ At Ungjin the allied generals argue about where to begin. One fortress sits where the road crosses the river, and most of the room wants it first.
[16] Black Tortoise: That fort is steep and strong. / Rush it and we bleed men. Sit under it and we bleed days. / Juryu is the nest. Pull the root, and the branches come down by themselves.
[17] ¶ So the armies split. Most of the generals take the land road. The Black Tortoise takes the water: a hundred and seventy warships, heading for the river mouth. On his deck stands Buyeo Yung.
[18] [MAP 663 Four banners, one river mouth: Tang by sea twice, Silla by land, and the East arriving in a hurry. Everyone is headed for the same mud.]
[19] ¶ Euija’s eldest. He knelt at Sabi three summers ago, was taken to Chang’an with his father, and has come back in a Tang officer’s coat to fight his younger brother for the right to tell the survivors what happened to them. Nobody on the deck says this. Everybody on the deck knows it.
[20] Black Tortoise: Your brother’s banner will be on that fleet. / When it comes, can you look at it?
[21] [CARD Prince Yung: Euija’s eldest son. Born to be crown prince. Born is not the same as stays.]
[22] Prince Yung: I have looked at worse. / …I looked at my father.
[23] ¶ The Black Tortoise has already learned the river's grammar. A narrow mouth. Sandbars that shift like lies. A current that punishes anyone who charges out of line. He anchors his hundred and seventy ships across the throat and waits. On the east bank, Kim Yushin's army keeps the shore from becoming a pier.
[24] ── SCENE: The Shore ──
[25] ¶ On the bank the Baekje horsemen guard the landing. They are the last mounted men the restoration can field, drawn up in front of the beached hulls the way you stand in front of a door you cannot afford to lose. Silla’s cavalry comes at them first, out ahead of the Tang foot, because the king of Silla wants it written down later who went first.
[26] Kim Yushin: Good riders. Guarding boats. / Men guard boats when they mean to leave in them.
[27] King Munmu: Riders. With me. / When they write this down in Chang’an, I want Silla in the first line.
[28] ¶ The shore camp goes in one charge. Yushin watches it from the ridge with the reins loose in one hand, which is how old generals watch something they no longer need to do themselves.
[29] ── SCENE: The Twenty-Seventh Day ──
[30] ¶ The first Yamato ships to arrive do not wait for the rest. They row straight at the Tang line on the evening water, and the Tang line does not move. It does not chase them, either. When the Yamato boats fall back, the hundred and seventy are exactly where they were that morning, in the same order, at anchor.
[31] ¶ The Black Tortoise has seen men of Wa once before, in the emperor's city. They were envoys in court silk, and they bowed in all the right places. The court kept them in a guesthouse for two winters, so they couldn't carry home where the fleet was going. These are their cousins. They row standing up. They shout from too far away. They charge a hundred and seventy anchored hulls in boats built for rice. Nobody in his army has fought them before. He watches the first wave break on his line like a scholar reading a new script. He is looking for the grammar.
[32] 🙇: General— those are Wa? They’re… / …they’re rowing standing up.
[33] Black Tortoise: The last Wa I saw were bowing to the Son of Heaven. / Watch their oars, not their faces. The faces will stay brave all day.
[34] Black Tortoise: Nobody chases. / Tomorrow they will all come back together, and they will come angry.
[35] ── SCENE: The Twenty-Eighth Day ──
[36] ¶ That night the Yamato captains and the king of Baekje hold council on a deck, and nobody looks at the sky. Abe no Hirafu does most of the talking. He is the rear general, a big man in a wolf-fur mantle who spent three summers chasing the Emishi along the cold northern coast, and he has the habit of men who have lived through bad water: he believes the sea gives way to whoever moves first.
[37] Abe no Hirafu: Yesterday was the vanguard. Today it’s all of us! / Ha— we go first. Whoever hits first, the other side gives way. That’s the sea. Every sea.
[38] Prince Pung: …Yes. First. / Let them see the king’s ship at the front.
[39] Echi no Takutsu: The tide turns before noon. / …Nobody is listening. Good. Then I will go first too.
[40] [FORMATION The Baekgang, eighth month, 663: Four charges into a formed Tang line, against the tide, in a river mouth too narrow for the eastern numbers. Smoke, flame, and a cinnabar sea.]
[41] ── SCENE: The Tide ──
[42] ¶ Takutsu’s ship is in the first line. His rowers pull standing. The Tang hulls come up out of the haze like a wall, and do not move.
[43] ¶ The first charge hits a wall of hulls and stops dead. Grapnels go over. Crossbows fire down from Tang decks built a man’s height higher. Takutsu’s men climb, fall back, and climb again.
[44] Echi no Takutsu: Back oars. Form again. / …The water is going slack.
[45] ¶ The second charge goes in on slack water and comes out against the ebb, the current turning against them. Now the river is pushing the eastern ships back onto each other. Hulls grind. Oars snap against a neighbour’s oars. Nobody can turn.
[46] ¶ On the Tang flagship, the Black Tortoise has waited all morning for exactly this. He says one word.
[47] Black Tortoise: Now.
[48] ¶ The arrows wrapped for flame go up white and come down burning. Ships pressed together turn one burning deck into a neighbourhood. On the third charge and the fourth, fire travels faster than orders. Four hundred eastern ships do not sink so much as spend themselves into light.
[49] ❝QUOTE (Jiu Tangshu (舊唐書) bk. 84, Liu Renkui (劉仁軌) — Battle of the White River mouth (663) · cf. Samguk Sagi bk. 28, Baekje Annals: 煙炎灼天 海水爲丹): They burned four hundred of their ships; smoke and flame filled the sky, and the seawater was all red.❞
[50] ¶ Then the wings close. The Tang ships that looked like a wall turn out to have been a door with two leaves, and they swing shut from left and right around the Yamato centre, so tight that the eastern ships cannot turn bow or stern, and men who cannot row and cannot climb go into the water in their armour.
[51] ¶ From the king’s ship Pung can see the Tang flagship. On its deck, in a Tang coat, stands his elder brother.
[52] Prince Pung: Yung… you wear their coat on our river…!
[53] Echi no Takutsu: Long live Kudara — Land of the Heavenly Deer….!
[54] ¶ His ship is burning under him and he does not leave it. He fights on the deck until there is not enough deck left to fight on.
[55] Echi no Takutsu: Baekje must survive….
[56] ❝QUOTE (Nihon Shoki (日本書紀) bk. 27, Tenji 2 (663), eighth month): Echi no Takutsu looked up to heaven and swore an oath, gnashed his teeth in fury, killed some dozens of men, and there fell in battle.❞
[57] Black Tortoise: Hold the line. Let the tide finish what the bowstrings began. / A river mouth is a judge. Today it judged the East.
[58] ¶ At the back of the fleet Abe no Hirafu’s ships are still afloat. He has seen a lost tide before, on a colder sea. He turns them for home and hauls in every swimmer the hulls will carry, men in half their armour, men with no oars, and he does not laugh again until Tsukushi.
[59] ── SCENE: Brothers ──
[60] ¶ In the smoke a small boat gets away from the king’s ship with a handful of men in it and turns north. It is Pung. He leaves behind his fleet, his allies, his capital on the hill, and his sword.
[61] ¶ They bring the sword to the Tang flagship. It is a Baekje ring-pommel blade with the ring worn smooth, nothing like a king’s, and the Black Tortoise hands it to the one man aboard who would know.
[62] Black Tortoise: Whose?
[63] Prince Yung: …My brother’s. / Our father gave it to him the year they sent him east. He was seven.
[64] Black Tortoise: Shall I send boats after him?
[65] Prince Yung: …North is Goguryeo. Let Goguryeo keep him. / He was always better at being sent away than I was.
[66] ── SCENE: Juryu ──
[67] ¶ Juryu holds ten more days without its king. Then it opens its gate. Pung’s younger brothers walk out at the head of what is left: soldiers, women, the Yamato men who missed the boats, and an envoy from **Tamla** who came up the hill to bargain for an island and is now surrendering for it.
[68] ¶ The people who are not surrendering go south, to the port where the Yamato ships will take them off. On the road they say the thing to one another that the Yamato chronicle wrote down, because nobody was left in Baekje to write it.
[69] ❝QUOTE (Nihon Shoki (日本書紀) bk. 27, Tenji 2 (663), ninth month): Juryu has surrendered. Nothing more can be done. The name of Baekje ends today. The place of our ancestors’ graves — how can we ever go back to it?❞
[70] ── SCENE: Imjon ──
[71] ¶ One fortress doesn’t hear it. Its commander shuts the gate and holds all autumn, and the siege goes home. Then two Baekje generals walk into the Tang camp and ask for their armour back.
[72] Black Tortoise: Heukchi Sangji. Your name is in my register already. / It reads better with you alive. Why now?
[73] Heukchi Sangji: I watched the king’s hands at Juryu. / Then I watched them row north.
[74] ¶ The Black Tortoise hands back their armour and points them up the slope.
[75] Heukchi Sangji: The north wall is the low one. / I built it.
[76] ¶ Imjon falls to its own people’s hands. Its commander leaves his wife and children inside and goes north to Goguryeo, which by now is where Baekje’s last kings go.
[77] ¶ When the water cools to ordinary colour again, the restoration has no fleet worth the word. The **Black Tortoise** sits down with Kim Yushin. Neither of them believes a word the other says, and they get a great deal done — which is how alliances sound after four hundred ships have paid for the silence.
[78] ¶ **Two reapers failed to take Yeon Gesomun at the river. The ledger still has his name in it…!**

=================================================================
#84 Yeon Gesomun†  (665)
Arc: The Final Stand · place: pyongyang · tone: deathbed drama
Logline: The Eternal General is dying.
=================================================================
[0] ── SCENE: King Yumla ──
[1] ¶ The Eternal General is dying.
[2] [MAP 665: ]
[3] ¶ He is sixty, which in his line of work is an insult to everyone he fought. The room in Pyongyang is small and too warm. His three sons stand at the bed. Gulgul stands by the door with his back to the wall. In his whole life he has never once sat with his back to a door.
[4] Yeon Gesomun: Do not… fight amongst yourselves…
[5] Yeon Namseng: Father. / You never kept a brother close. / One you sent to the far end of the southern border. The rest you cut down.
[6] Yeon Gesomun: …That is precisely why I am telling you.
[7] Yeon Namsan: …He means it, brother.
[8] Yeon Namseng: He always means it. That has never been the trouble.
[9] ¶ Then he does something nobody in the room expects. He sits up.
[10] Yeon Gesomun: Gulgul. The chair. Put me in the chair. / I’m not meeting anybody lying down.
[11] ¶ Gulgul carries him across the room like a sack of grain he is fond of. The swords go on the wall behind the chair, all five, where a visitor will see them.
[12] Yeon Gesomun: I said it once. Until every bone in me is broken. / Count them, Gulgul. How many are left?
[13] Gulgul: Enough, sir.
[14] ¶ He expects one of them — Kangrim with his Question, or Haewonmek with his last words. He has been rehearsing a refusal.
[15] Yeon Gesomun: …Which of you failed me at the Snake River? / Come on. Ask. I am ready to say no again.
[16] ¶ It is not either of them. Purple of sentence, not crow-dark of the fetch — **Yumla** himself stands in the room. The judge, not the clerks. A king for a king.
[17] Yumla: Yeon Gesomun. / My two best men could not bring you at the Snake River. / A man like you — only another king could carry you off. / Consider the courtesy returned.
[18] Yeon Gesomun: …Hah. / So the clerks failed, and the boss clocked in. / Fine. I always preferred dealing with the top.
[19] Yumla: The minutes will remember the joke. / Now — walk. Judgment keeps better hours than Supreme Commanders.
[20] Yeon Gesomun: One thing first. My sons—
[21] Yumla: Are not my department. / …Yet.
[22] ¶ At the very end Yeon catches a vision of something. A young man, centuries off, standing in a gate and saying Goryeo as if it had never gone.
[23] Yeon Gesomun: …Goguryeo, you idiot. Say the whole thing.
[24] ¶ Then he dies in his sleep, sitting up, which is not how anyone expected it to go.
[25] Yeon Namseng: Well… even a man like that stands before Yumla in the end.
[26] ¶ His eldest, Namseng, takes on the title of Supreme Commander. He is thirty-one, and it is very heavy.
[27] [CARD Yeon Namseng: His father’s chair. It was built for one man, and it shows.]
[28] ── SCENE: The Chair ──
[29] ¶ Namseng sits in the chair the next morning. It is too big. Everyone pretends not to notice, which is how you know they have.
[30] Yeon Namgun: The old man… he really did have a gift, didn’t he.
[31] Yeon Namsan: He had one. We don’t.
[32] ¶ Gulgul does not sit at all. He rides north that afternoon, to the border the old man gave him. Nobody tells him to.
[33] ¶ He outlasted the Second Emperor’s war. He broke the White Tiger in the Snake River with his own hands. Every victory made the kingdom lean on him a little harder, until the whole weight of it rested on one man’s spine. A spine is a magnificent thing. No one has ever built a house on one.
[34] ¶ Once, three men looked up at the same star and wanted the same thing. He is the last of them to go.
[35] ¶ **“Do not fight amongst yourselves.” He had three sons. How long do you think that lasts?**

=================================================================
#85 Brothers’ Coup  (666 December)
Arc: The Final Stand · place: pyongyang · tone: succession thriller
Logline: Three brothers, one seal, and men whispering in both directions.
=================================================================
[0] ¶ Nine months. That is how long it lasts.
[1] ── SCENE: The Provinces ──
[2] ¶ In the spring Namseng rides out to tour the provinces, as a new Supreme Commander should. He leaves his two younger brothers to keep the capital.
[3] ¶ Within a month there are men whispering in both directions. To Namgun and Namsan: your brother means to be rid of you when he comes back. To Namseng, at every post station: your brothers do not mean to let you back in.
[4] Yeon Namseng: Nonsense. They are my brothers. / …Send someone back anyway. Quietly. I want to know what they say at supper.
[5] ── SCENE: The Pyongyang Gate ──
[6] ¶ The man he sends is caught at the Pyongyang gate within the week. Namgun reads the orders found on him twice, and the second time he reads them as a confession.
[7] Yeon Namgun: He sends spies. To his own brothers. / Shut the gates! Tell the king the Supreme Commander has rebelled!
[8] ¶ Namseng’s son is in the capital that spring, with his mother. He is nine years old and wears a little gold ring his grandfather gave him.
[9] ── SCENE: The Shut Gate ──
[10] ¶ He rides back to his own capital and finds the gate shut. His brother comes up onto the wall.
[11] Yeon Namseng: Open the gate, Namgun. / You are speaking to the Supreme Commander.
[12] Yeon Namgun: Supreme Commander! You send spies to your brothers’ supper and call it command!
[13] Yeon Namseng: I sent a man to ask how you were. You hanged him.
[14] Yeon Namseng: Namgun. Look at me. At the Liao, who took the flogging?
[15] Yeon Namgun: …You did.
[16] Yeon Namseng: And why?
[17] Yeon Namgun: Because you’re the elder. You’ve been the elder every single day since. / And they told me you were coming back with a seal for my head.
[18] Yeon Namseng: And you believed them. Traitor.
[19] Yeon Namgun: Traitor…? Me?
[20] Yeon Namseng: Open the gate. My wife is in there. My son—
[21] ¶ Namgun does not answer. He looks at Namsan. Namsan looks at the ground.
[22] ¶ Something small comes over the wall and lands in the mud at the horse’s feet. A gold ring, a child’s size.
[23] Yeon Namgun: He was carrying a letter to you. Out through the water gate. / The guards didn’t— I didn’t—
[24] ¶ Namseng gets down from his horse and picks the ring out of the mud. He wipes it on his sleeve. He does not look at the wall again.
[25] ¶ That night he rides north to the old capital at Gungnae. From there he sends his other son west, to Chang’an, to ask the Third Emperor for an army.
[26] ── SCENE: Defection of Yeon Namseng ──
[27] ¶ Namseng rides west, across the river his father spent a lifetime holding.
[28] [MAP 666: North to the old capital, then west over the Liao. His father spent a lifetime stopping men riding this road the other way.]
[29] ── SCENE: Chang’an ──
[30] Yeon Namseng: Goryeo is nothing but swindlers and thieves — / a people beyond hope.
[31] The Third Emperor: …My father spoke of a boy he met at the Liao. / One who would not kneel.
[32] Yeon Namseng: Twenty years ago, Majesty. Your father and I, when he crossed the Liao. / I did not kneel then.
[33] ¶ He is thirty-two years old, and his brother has taken his title, his city and his father’s seat, and this is the second time in his life he has been offered a house in Chang’an. Nobody flogs him for the answer this time.
[34] Yeon Namseng: Your Majesty will never conquer Samhan alone.
[35] Yeon Namseng: Emperor… Your Majesty… ten thousand years…!
[36] ¶ Namseng is given a Tang title, and a vanguard command against his own country.
[37] ¶ The Third Emperor has wanted this war since he was a boy, watching his father come home from it. Now it arrives with a guide.
[38] ¶ In the south their uncle **Yeon Jungto**, who raised two of them, waits to hear which nephew will send for him. Neither does. He takes twelve cities over to Silla, and the family is finished in three directions at once.
[39] ¶ Years later, in the emperor’s country, Namseng’s tombstone will tell the story his way.
[40] ❝QUOTE (Epitaph of Yeon Namseng (泉男生墓誌) — Luoyang, 679; transcription in the Korean Ancient History DB (한국 고대 사료 DB)): His heart was loyal, but matters went wrong at the centre. He had just gone out to comfort the border folk and tour the wild marches, to survey the old lands of the dawn country and ask for new officers to govern them. Then his two younger brothers, Namsan and Namgun, turned vicious and rebellious in a single morning. Heartless to their own blood, they raised troops and shut him out from within. His little son with the gold ring fell suddenly into the whale's jaws, and left the long table and his parents' arms for ever.❞
[41] ¶ **Namseng knows the road in. Now he rides it home, with the whole Tang army at his back…!**

=================================================================
#86 Pyongyang II  (668 September)
Arc: The Final Stand · place: pyongyang · tone: grim war epic — the siege
Logline: When the ring closes, the city needs one man nobody can buy. They pick a monk.
=================================================================
[0] ¶ Every son comes home in the end. Namseng brings the empire with him.
[1] ── SCENE: The Ninth Invasion ──
[2] ¶ Three of the emperor’s four beasts come for the city at once. The Blue Dragon leads, the old marshal who has been at this war since the last emperor. The Black Tortoise and the second White Tiger ride behind him.
[3] [MAP 667: Three beasts, three roads, one city.]
[4] Xue Rengui: Breaking a fortress… is like farming. / You know the season, you bring the water, you harvest. / Today is a harvest day.
[5] ¶ There is no cruelty in him, which is precisely what makes him difficult: the men of Goguryeo can hate a butcher, but they cannot quite hate a farmer who treats siege-work as weather.
[6] ── SCENE: Brothers ──
[7] ¶ Namseng rides beside the Blue Dragon in a Tang coat, to show him the road. He knows every gully. He used to hunt them. At the top of the last one he reins in and looks at the red gate.
[8] Yeon Namseng: At last… I set foot on Pyongyang’s ground—
[9] ¶ On the wall, Namgun can see him. Everyone on the wall can see him.
[10] [CARD Yeon Namsan: Gesomun’s youngest son, and the one who listens at doors.]
[11] Yeon Namsan: Brother… he’s wearing their coat.
[12] Yeon Namgun: Goguryeo… never dies….!
[13] ¶ That is the only conversation the three of them have that year. A whisper, a shout, and a man on a horse who does not answer.
[14] ── SCENE: The White Banner ──
[15] ¶ The ring closes. A month goes by. Inside, the granaries go down the way the Tang campfires did, seven winters ago, and someone on the wall is counting.
[16] ¶ Namsan counts best. So it is Namsan who walks out first.
[17] ¶ He goes out through the gate with the king and ninety-eight officials, carrying a white banner. The king of Goguryeo has worn the crown twenty-six years. For most of them a Yeon told him what to say. Today a Yeon is telling him again.
[18] King Bojang: Do I— do I kneel to him, or to the banner?
[19] Yeon Namsan: To the banner, Majesty. He’s only holding it.
[20] ¶ The king kneels. The Blue Dragon accepts the surrender very politely. Then he looks up at the walls, where the gate has already shut again behind them.
[21] ── SCENE: Betrayal from Inside ──
[22] ¶ Namgun has not surrendered. He has the walls, the army and the gate. What he needs is one man nobody can buy. He picks a monk. Shinsung has kept a small temple at the foot of the hill for twenty-five years. He has never asked anyone for anything.
[23] Yeon Namgun: You have no clan, no faction, no sons. / You’re the only man in this city I can’t imagine selling it.
[24] Shinsung: Then I shall try to be worthy of your imagination, Mangniji.
[25] ¶ For five days a novice walks out of the lesser house before dawn with an alms bowl and comes back with it empty, and nobody thinks to ask why a monk’s bowl should come back empty from the direction of the Tang lines. On the fifth night the bell that has sat on the floor of the lesser house since the year the Daoists came is struck once.
[26] ¶ Yeon once tried to starve the temples with the emperor’s Daoists. The monks have waited a generation. Shinsung doesn’t make a speech about doctrine. He opens a gate.
[27] ¶ The Tang come in before the bell has stopped ringing. Quietly at first, then not quietly at all. The gate towers catch one after another, like lamps being lit for a feast.
[28] ── SCENE: Last Words ──
[29] ¶ Namgun is thirty-one. He leads the last stand against the Blue Dragon himself.
[30] Yeon Namgun: Silla’s sacred blood — rot! / Goguryeo will take the final victory! / You may rule this soil — our name will have the last word!
[31] ¶ The wall is already lost. He knows it. He says it anyway, to the men who can still hear, and to a bloodline across the river he can’t see.
[32] Yeon Namgun: Goguryeo… never dies….!
[33] ¶ When the gate towers burn, Namgun stabs himself in his own hall. He does it badly, the first thing he has done badly in the whole war, and the Tang surgeons save him so that he can be sent alive to the farthest edge of the empire.
[34] ¶ In the burning palace, a Mohe man with a border sabre walks into a treasury nobody is guarding any more. He comes out with a piece of gold no longer than a finger, snapped off something that used to be worn on a head. Nobody stops him. Nobody ever looks at Gulgul.
[35] ¶ Among the captives is a Baekje king with a Yamato accent. Pung ran north to the last kingdom left. The kingdoms ran out before he did.
[36] ¶ When the city falls, the empire doesn't send a stranger to hold it. It sends Xue Rengui. The white coat becomes a banner over a broken capital. He governs well enough that even the conquered prefer him to chaos.
[37] Xue Rengui: I… did not wish to be your enemy. / But I could not leave His Majesty’s east empty-handed.
[38] ¶ Goguryeo had stood seven hundred years. The record, for its part, writes only the month and the surrender.
[39] ── SCENE: Zhaoling ──
[40] ¶ Before the captives are shown to the living emperor, the Blue Dragon takes them up the mountain to show them to the dead one. The king of Goguryeo is made to bow at Zhaoling, in front of the door the Second Emperor said his horses would guard. The six stone horses stand in their row. The purple one is nearest the door.
[41] ── SCENE: The New Rank ──
[42] ¶ The seventeen grades stop at one another. In the tenth month, after the city is open, **King Munmu** cuts a rank the grades did not have, and gives it to the man who has been Marshal since the yard.
[43] King Munmu: Marshal.
[44] Kim Yushin: Majesty.
[45] King Munmu: You have been Marshal since before I could hold a bow. / The yard still says it. / The seventeen grades do not reach you anymore.
[46] Kim Yushin: The word is enough. / I know what I am.
[47] King Munmu: There was already a grade above the seventeen. / I had them cut one above that. / Supreme General.
[48] [CARD Kim Yushin: A rank above every rank. They had to invent it for him.]
[49] Kim Yushin: A new name for an old man.
[50] King Munmu: It is the name of the man who fed this war through the snow. / Wear it. / You may keep Marshal for the boys on the yard.
[51] Kim Yushin: …As you command.
[52] ¶ **The story isn’t over yet. The Third Emperor still controls large swaths of Samhan. The final war begins…!**

=================================================================
#87 Mount Gain  (665 August)
Arc: Silla-Tang War · tone: oath and grief
Logline: The night Pyongyang falls, Munmu goes to look at an oath. Three summers earlier, the empire made him swear it over his uncle’s white horse.
=================================================================
[0] ── SCENE: The Ancestral Temple ──
[1] ¶ The night Pyongyang falls, the king of Silla goes to visit a piece of paper.
[2] ¶ It hangs in the ancestral temple, beside his father's tablet. Gold letters on iron. An oath, sworn over a dead horse, to love Baekje's prince like a brother. Goguryeo is gone tonight. Up north, the emperor's clerks are already measuring what is left.
[3] King Munmu: Everything south of Pyongyang, and the whole of Baekje. / My father made me learn it by heart.
[4] Kim Yushin: The emperor will have learned a sentence too, Majesty.
[5] King Munmu: I know. It’s hanging right here. / Uncle. Do you remember the horse?
[6] Kim Yushin: …Every day, Majesty.
[7] ¶ Every war starts with an insult somebody swallowed. Silla swallowed this one three summers ago. To taste it, go back to a hill outside Bear Ford, and the only white horse in the camp.
[8] ── SCENE: Bear Ford, Three Summers Earlier ──
[9] ¶ Two springs after the White River, the empire names a governor for what is left of Baekje. It is Buyeo Yung. He once knelt at Bupmin's horse and was spat on. Then he went to the emperor's city and came back in imperial robes. Now he will rule from the fortress where his father was arrested.
[10] ¶ The court in Surabol hears the name and goes very quiet. Their men died for this ground. An emperor promised it to Chunchu by lamplight. Now a Baekje prince sits on it again, with the emperor's seal in his hand.
[11] ¶ Yung moves into the commandery offices in the spring. The rooms his father was taken from have been whitewashed. The Black Tortoise shows him the registers, and the calendar, and the list of names he may not write.
[12] Black Tortoise: Your households, Commander. Every one of them a number now. It makes them much easier to look after.
[13] Prince Yung: …My father counted them by name. / He was wrong about most things. Not that.
[14] ── SCENE: The Altar ──
[15] ¶ That summer, the empire makes the two men who rule the south swear to be brothers. It picks a hill outside Bear Ford. The clerks name it the Mountain Where One Goes for Gain. They mean it kindly.
[16] [PLACE chwiri: A hill outside Bear Ford, named by optimists.]
[17] ¶ An imperial envoy presides. The Black Tortoise wrote the oath. On one side of the altar stands Munmu. On the other stands Yung. Munmu last saw that face at the height of his horse's knees.
[18] ── SCENE: The White Horse ──
[19] ¶ An oath of this weight needs a white horse. The Tang adjutant has been walking the Silla lines all morning looking for one, and stops in front of the only white horse in the camp.
[20] Tang adjutant: That one. Whose is he?
[21] ¶ Hanseul is past twenty. He has carried Yushin across the Yellow Mountain. He has carried rice through snow up to his chest. His muzzle has gone grey. On a white horse, only the man who feeds him notices.
[22] King Munmu: No. Find another. That is my uncle’s—
[23] Kim Yushin: Let them have him, Majesty.
[24] King Munmu: Uncle.
[25] Kim Yushin: A white horse is what they asked for. It would be a poor oath on a brown one. / …I’ll walk him up myself.
[26] ¶ He leads Hanseul up the hill by the halter, the way he led Hangyul across the Moon Palace yard eighteen years before, talking to him in the low voice he keeps for horses and uses on no one else. At the altar he holds the head himself.
[27] ¶ The knife is Tang. The blood goes into a bowl, and both men touch it to their lips. Yung does it without looking at anyone. Munmu does it looking at his uncle’s hands.
[28] Black Tortoise: …Let them be as brothers, sharing disaster and pitying each other’s sorrows, forever as one. / Whoever breaks this covenant, may the gods see it; may a hundred calamities fall on him, may his sons not grow, and may no one remain to keep his altars.
[29] ¶ The covenant is written out three times. One copy is buried at the altar with the horse. One goes to Chang’an. The third is carried to Surabol and laid up in Silla’s ancestral temple, where the kings of Silla will have to walk past it every time they visit their fathers.
[30] ── SCENE: Surabol ──
[31] ¶ On the road home nobody in the Silla column says anything about the horse.
[32] ¶ In Surabol the anger is louder. Men bled for this land in three wars. An emperor promised it to them. Now they have sworn on a dead horse never to take it. The young officers say betrayal in the barracks. The older ones say nothing. They start counting Tang garrisons.
[33] ¶ That night the king finds his uncle in the stable, cleaning a stall that is empty.
[34] King Munmu: I’ll find you another white horse, Uncle.
[35] Kim Yushin: I’m seventy, Majesty. I’ve buried three. / Find me a war instead. I’d like to go to one more before they make me swear to something else.
[36] ── SCENE: The Ancestral Temple ──
[37] ¶ Three summers later, the old man got his war. It ended tonight, with a monk at a gate. He stands beside the king in the temple now, and neither of them looks at the iron for long.
[38] King Munmu: Uncle. Before the emperors. Before seals, and oaths, and governors with lists. / Who was the first king of this land?
[39] Kim Yushin: Ask your mother. She tells it to every child in the house. / It starts with a bear.
[40] King Munmu: A bear.
[41] Kim Yushin: A patient one. Your mother always looks at me when she gets to that part.
[42] ¶ **To find the first king of this land, we have to go back before there were kingdoms… to a bear in a cave…!**
