#88 Dangun & Old Joseon  (Long ago)  [FLASHBACK EPISODE]
Arc: Silla-Tang War · place: asadal · tone: founder fairy tale, then a dark legend
Logline: Before there are any kingdoms, there is a son in heaven who keeps looking down.
=================================================================
[0] ¶ Before there are any kingdoms, there is a son in heaven who keeps looking down. He is **Hwanung**. His father **Hwanin**, the Lord of Heaven, notices, looks down himself at a mountain called Taebaek and the people living around it, and decides the world could use his son.
[1] [CARD Hwanin: The Lord of Heaven. He has been watching this peninsula since before it had names.]
[2] [DIAGRAM joseon-mandate Old Joseon · 고조선 — Heaven’s mandate made into a capital: Hwanin → Hwanung → Dangun → Asadal.]
[3] ¶ Hwanin does not plough — he opens the sky. Three seals go down with his son, so that nobody on the ground can mistake him for a prince playing at exile. Every later king in this chronicle will cut seals of his own, and every one of them is copying these.
[4] ¶ Hwanung lands on a mountain under the sacred birch. He names the ground beneath it the Divine City. Three thousand followers come down with him. Among them are the lords of wind, rain and cloud. Someone has to argue with the weather.
[5] [CARD Hwanung: Hwanung. A son of heaven who kept looking down until his father let him go.]
[6] ¶ From there he hands out civilisation in instalments. Laws. Punishments. Lifespans. Illness. Good and evil. Medicine. Three hundred and sixty matters in all. Somebody counted.
[7] ¶ There is a short way to tell the rest, the way it is carved on stones. The long way begins, as long ways do, with a bear who wanted something so badly that she outlasted a tiger for it.
[8] ¶ A bear and a tiger come to him and ask to be made human. He gives them a bundle of mugwort, twenty cloves of garlic, and one instruction: stay out of the sun for a hundred days.
[9] ── SCENE: The Sacred Birch ──
[10] ¶ The bear stays. She comes out a woman on the twenty-first morning, garlic still on her breath, and finds the mountain already staffed — wind, rain, cloud, and not one of them a husband. So she stands under the sacred tree. Not once. Every day, on the path he has to take if he means to reach the hall.
[11] [CARD Ungnyeo: Ungnyeo. Twenty-one days in a cave, and the tiger left first. A husband should be easy.]
[12] ¶ He means to reach the hall. On the third evening he gets as far as the birch, and the seal in his hand becomes a thing he is holding for no reason he can name.
[13] Ungnyeo: You're going to walk past again.
[14] Hwanung: …Not today.
[15] Ungnyeo: Yesterday you did. / And the day before. I was standing right here.
[16] Hwanung: I saw you. / The garlic reached this far.
[17] Ungnyeo: Twenty-one days of that, and this is what came out. / …I was going to say don't come closer.
[18] Hwanung: Too late. / Stay. I mean— don't go. Your hand—
[19] Ungnyeo: You already have the hand. / …Scared of the rest?
[20] Hwanung: I am. / Because you're looking at me.
[21] Ungnyeo: Then come down. / The tree can watch. I want… more.
[22] ¶ The kiss is clumsy. Beard, a new mouth, birch bark at her back. She makes a small furious sound and tries again, and the second one lands.
[23] ¶ White silk goes down among the roots. The fur at her throat opens under his mouth. She laughs once, startled at the sound, and pulls him down by the hair.
[24] ¶ By the time the moon clears the snow on the peak, the rust-red sash is somewhere in the moss, and neither of them has gone back up the path.
[25] Ungnyeo: …You're going already?
[26] Hwanung: I can't. / I don't know where I put the seal.
[27] Ungnyeo: Under my head. / I took it. …Don't go.
[28] Hwanung: …Thief.
[29] Ungnyeo: Marry me in the morning. / Right now I'm here.
[30] ── SCENE: Asadal ──
[31] ¶ Their son is Dangun. The name on the stone is Wanggeom: a king who governs, not one who inherits a bone rank. He founds Asadal where the mountain meets the plain. He rules for fifteen hundred years, and then he becomes the mountain.
[32] [CARD Dangun: Dangun. Half heaven, half bear, and all the paperwork of a first king.]
[33] ❝QUOTE (Samguk Yusa (三國遺事) bk. 1, Wonder 1 — Old Joseon (Dangun); Ha & Mintz tr., pp. 32–33): He granted three heavenly seals and sent him to govern. Hwanung led a following of three thousand and descended under the sacred altar-tree on the summit of Mount Taebaek; this was called the Divine City. He married the bear-woman, and she bore a son named Dangun Wanggeom.❞
[34] [PLACE asadal: Where the mountain meets the plain, and the first crown met both.]
[35] ¶ Every later crown in these kingdoms argues, one way or another, back to the woman who used to be a bear. Her son’s city keeps his name long after he has become a mountain.
[36] ── SCENE: The Fall of Joseon ──
[37] ¶ Joseon outlives its founder by a long way. Two thousand years on it is still there, run by other kings now, from a walled city on the Taedong that has kept his name: **Wanggeom**. In the autumn of 109 BC, Han comes to the gate.
[38] ¶ It takes the empire of the West a year to take one fortress, and they do not take it. Wanggeom holds through a siege that begins in the autumn and is still going the following autumn.
[39] ¶ So they stop attacking the walls and start talking to the men behind them, which is cheaper and has never once failed.
[40] ── SCENE: The King's Wall ──
[41] ¶ **King Ugeo** has stopped sleeping in the palace. He sleeps on the wall, where he can hear the Han camp coughing, and his son, the prince, has started sleeping somewhere else.
[42] Prince Jang Hang: Father. They’ve sent terms again. / Open the gate, they say, and nobody inside gets hurt.
[43] King Ugeo: They said that last autumn. / Who brought it to you?
[44] Prince Jang Hang: …Does it matter who?
[45] King Ugeo: It matters. / Get off my wall.
[46] ¶ One of the ministers who have been doing the talking goes over the wall that week and dies on the road before he reaches the Han tents. Another does not bother with the road. One night at the start of summer he sends men up the wall-stair instead.
[47] Seong Gi: Majesty—!
[48] King Ugeo: …Seong Gi? / Don’t hold the city. Not for me. / Get the people out. Live… and make a new country. Anywhere.
[49] ¶ Seong Gi closes the king’s eyes, goes back up to the parapet, and holds the city anyway.
[50] ¶ He holds it until the dead minister’s son and the prince go down into the lanes, where people have been eating bark since the spring.
[51] Choi: The king is dead. / So who are you starving for now? Him?
[52] ¶ Before morning Seong Gi is dead too.
[53] ¶ Someone lifts the bar.
[54] The Herald: The wall did not come down.
[55] The Herald: A door was opened from the inside.
[56] ¶ Han takes Wanggeom. Some of the people the king told to live go south over the mountains. They settle in six villages around Surabol. Two generations later, they'll go looking for a king. The rest stay, and the empire cuts them into four pieces. The last piece is still collecting taxes four hundred years later.
[57] ¶ That is the story Munmu gets, in his mother’s version, with extra garlic. He came for the bear. He keeps thinking about the door.
[58] ¶ **Eight hundred years later, the empire comes back to the same river to do the same thing. This time, Goguryeo has a prince left…!**

=================================================================
#89 Anseung  (670 June)
Arc: Silla-Tang War · place: pyongyang · tone: exile court drama
Logline: Geom Mojam raises Goguryeo’s flag and finds a royal to stand under it. They disagree about dying, and only one of them sees the morning.
=================================================================
[0] ── SCENE: The Protectorate ──
[1] ¶ Every revival needs two things: a flag and a royal. Geom Mojam has the flag.
[2] ¶ The empire has done it again on the Taedong. Pyongyang is a Protectorate now, run by Tang clerks who seem surprised that anyone minds. Mojam minds. He kills the clerks, raises Goguryeo’s colours, and goes looking for someone royal to stand under them.
[3] ¶ He finds one on an island in the western sea, mending a net. His name is Anseung. His father is Yeon Jungto, the uncle who took twelve cities over to Silla. His mother was a king’s daughter. Mojam only needs the second half.
[4] ❝QUOTE (Samguk Sagi (三國史記) bk. 6, Silla Annals — King Munmu, yr. 10 (670), sixth month): Mojam, a daehyeong of Goguryeo from Surim Fortress, gathered the surviving people, marched from Gungmo Fortress to south of the Pae River, and killed the Tang officials and the monk Beop'an. Heading for Silla, he reached Saya Island in the western sea, found Anseung, son of the Goguryeo minister Yeon Jungto, brought him into the River Palace, and set him up as lord.❞
[5] ── SCENE: The River Camp ──
[6] ¶ By the next spring the revival has a court, a royal, and four thousand households camped along the river. It also has a Tang army coming down the north road. The two men argue about it in front of everyone, because a revival has no rooms with doors.
[7] Geom Mojam: We hold the river. We hold Pyongyang. / If they want it back, they can climb over us.
[8] Anseung: They climbed over Pyongyang two years ago. With better walls than ours in the way.
[9] Geom Mojam: Pyongyang has kings in its soil four hundred years deep. You want to leave them for a Silla guest room?
[10] Anseung: The kings in the soil will keep. The four thousand households above it won’t.
[11] Geom Mojam: Then go. Take your households. / I’ll hold it with whoever stays.
[12] ¶ He says it loud, to the fires. Around the fires, men stop eating. Anseung looks at them. Nobody stands up. Nobody sits down either. He understands what that means before Mojam does. In the morning they will follow whoever is still alive.
[13] Anseung: …You’re right, General. / Let’s sleep on it.
[14] ¶ That night Anseung has him killed in his tent. It is the first Goguryeo blood the revival spills, and it is spilled by Goguryeo.
[15] ¶ In the morning the men by the fires do not ask where the general is. They pack.
[16] ¶ Then he takes four thousand households south, to Silla.
[17] ── SCENE: Silla's Guest ──
[18] ¶ Munmu gives him a title, a district, and a name for the thing: Goguryeo, still standing, inside Silla. It is a useful fiction and both sides know exactly how useful.
[19] ¶ Silla settles him in a town that was somebody else's kingdom ten years ago. Within the year he is called King of Goguryeo. In time he gets a bride, and a seat at Munmu's feasts. Well below the king's.
[20] King Munmu: A king of Goguryeo in Silla. The emperor will hate it. / Good. Give him a seal. A big one.
[21] King Munmu: And end the patent the way the emperor ends his. “Be reverent.” / Twice. He’ll hate that most of all.
[22] ¶ Anseung bows when the seal comes, very low: a king of Goguryeo in a Silla hall. Far north, on the Taedong, a tent is still standing with nobody in it.
[23] ¶ **The emperor hears there is a king of Goguryeo in Silla. His general reaches for a brush instead of a sword…!**

=================================================================
#90 Letters  (671 July)
Arc: Silla-Tang War · tone: epistolary duel
Logline: Xue Rengui would like to win this war by post. The king does not go to bed.
=================================================================
[0] ── SCENE: The First Letter ──
[1] ¶ In high summer, a Tang monk is rowed ashore under a white flag. He carries a letter from the fleet. The fleet belongs to Xue Rengui, the second White Tiger. He has sat off the coast all summer. If it can be managed, he'd like to win this war by post.
[2] Imyun: The Commander sends his respects, Majesty. He asks that it be read aloud. / He says it reads better aloud.
[3] Xue Rengui: To the King of Silla, from Xue Rengui, Commander of the Eastern Fleet, greetings. / A clear wind blows ten thousand li from the capital to your coast, and the sea between is three thousand. I have come all of it to say one thing. / Your father knelt before the Second Emperor and was raised up. He was given robes, and a brother, and an army. You were given his crown. / And now you take the land the emperor’s soldiers bled for, and you shelter his rebels, and your own brother waits in Chang’an, ashamed to be asked about you. / Turn back while there is still a road to turn on. / I have the honour to remain, in all things but this, Your Majesty’s servant — / Xue Rengui.
[4] ¶ The copy the archives keep is longer, and has a cicada in it.
[5] ❝QUOTE (Samguk Sagi (三國史記) bk. 7, Silla Annals — King Munmu, yr. 11 (671), seventh month — Xue Rengui's letter, carried by the monk Imyun) [Xue Rengui]: It is like a man who goes out with his sling and never sees the dry well at his feet, or reaches for the cicada and never knows the oriole is behind him. That is Your Majesty, not knowing your own measure. … Alas! Once loyal and righteous, now a rebel subject. I grieve that what began in good fortune ends in ill, that what grew from one root ends in different branches. The wind is high and the air is sharp; the leaves fall and the year turns sad. I lean on the mountain and look far off, and it wounds my heart.❞
[6] ¶ The monk is given a bed, a meal, and as long as it takes. The king does not go to bed at all.
[7] ── SCENE: The Writing Room ──
[8] ¶ By the second night the king’s writing room is full of men with opinions. One of them, an official named **Daeto**, has more than most.
[9] Daeto: Majesty, a softer word here and there costs nothing. / They have a fleet off Bear Ford. They have Prince Inmun. Could we not say we were mistaken about the border? Everyone is mistaken about borders.
[10] King Munmu: We were not mistaken. / Write it the way I say it.
[11] ¶ There is another reason the room is careful. Nine summers ago, the king killed a great lord and his whole house for calling in sick. The lord's son wasn't in the house. He's in the emperor's guard. Somebody there will have told him by now.
[12] ── SCENE: The Reply ──
[13] King Munmu: To the Commander of the Eastern Fleet, from the King of Silla. / Your letter came by a monk, and was read aloud as you asked. It does read better aloud. So will this.
[14] ¶ He dictates the rest standing up, and does not stop for most of the night.
[15] King Munmu: In the twenty-second year of Zhenguan my father went to Chang’an. The Second Emperor took him into a gallery of stone horses and said: everything south of Pyongyang, and the whole of Baekje, shall be Silla’s, forever. / My father made me learn those words when I was twenty-two. I have them still. I expect the emperor’s clerks have them too.
[16] King Munmu: When your Red Fowl sat outside Pyongyang eating his horses, my uncle was sixty-seven. He walked beside his own white horse through snow to its chest so the horse could carry rice instead of him. Your soldiers wept when they saw the carts. Your general took the rice and sailed home the same week. / We were late, he said. We are always late. We came anyway.
[17] King Munmu: Then you gave Baekje back to a Baekje prince, with a Tang seal, at Bear Ford. Then you took us up a hill called Gain and made us swear to be his brother over a dead horse. / The horse was my uncle’s. He walked it up himself. I watched his hands.
[18] King Munmu: At Pyongyang our men went through the gate first. Then your Protectorate came and wrote our share down as nothing. / You say I shelter rebels. I shelter the people your officials could not be bothered to count.
[19] ❝QUOTE (Samguk Sagi (三國史記) bk. 7, Silla Annals — King Munmu, yr. 11 (671), seventh month — King Munmu's reply to Xue Rengui) [King Munmu]: Alas! While the two kingdoms stood, we were the hounds that ran at your pointing finger. Now the game is all taken, and it is we who are threatened with the pot. Baekje, the bandits' leavings, is rewarded the way Han once paid off an old enemy; Silla, which died for Han, is cut down the way Han once killed a man for sparing it. Though the sun's light no longer turns our way, the sunflower's heart still faces the sun.❞
[20] King Munmu: My brother is in Chang’an. Tell him I am well. Tell him I said his name. / I have the honour to remain the king of the country you came to save — / Bupmin.
[21] ¶ Daeto copies it out fair. His hand is very steady. Later that night he writes a second letter, a short one, to a different address, and puts it in his sleeve, and does not send it yet.
[22] ── SCENE: The Second Letter ──
[23] Xue Rengui: Your Majesty’s letter has been received, and read aloud. It took most of an afternoon. / Nowhere in it is the word “sorry.” / I have the honour to remain your servant, in fewer things than before — / Xue.
[24] King Munmu: The Commander’s letter has been received. It took no time at all. / Nowhere in it is the word “rice.” / I have the honour to remain the king — / B.
[25] Xue Rengui: Then I will come and fetch the apology myself. / — X.
[26] King Munmu: Come, then. / — B.
[27] ── SCENE: Seventy Ships ──
[28] ¶ He comes. In the tenth month, off the western coast, a Silla squadron finds seventy Tang transports riding low with grain for the garrison at Bear Ford, and takes them: hulls, crews, one Tang colonel, and all of the rice.
[29] ❝QUOTE (Samguk Sagi (三國史記) bk. 7, Silla Annals — King Munmu, yr. 11 (671), tenth month): Winter, the sixth day of the tenth month: we struck more than seventy Tang grain transports and captured the colonel Qianer Dahou and over a hundred soldiers. The drowned were past counting. The geupchan Dangcheon's merit was first, and he was raised to sachan.❞
[30] King Munmu: Send word to the White Tiger that his rice has arrived. / Late. As usual.
[31] ¶ **The Tang are coming south. Silla is winning. That is exactly when armies start to chase…!**

=================================================================
#91 Stone Gate  (672 August)
Arc: Silla-Tang War · place: seokmun · tone: grim war epic
Logline: Silla wins the morning, then makes the mistake that costs the year: it chases.
=================================================================
[0] ── SCENE: Stone Gate ──
[1] ¶ Winning is the most dangerous thing an army can do.
[2] ¶ Silla and what is left of the Goguryeo revival meet the Tang coming south, break them, and cut down several thousand. By noon the Tang are running north. Soon after, Silla is running after them.
[3] [MAP 672: The Tang come south and turn. Silla gives chase. Watch where the chase ends.]
[4] ¶ Among the riders is a lieutenant barely old enough for the rank, with a famous father and a borrowed horse. His name is **Wonsul**. Like every boy in his father’s yard, he has been taught that a Hwarang does not retreat. Nobody has taught him where a chase ends.
[5] Danneung: Lieutenant. The column’s strung out over two li. We’re not in line.
[6] Wonsul: They’re running. You don’t form a line to chase a man who’s running.
[7] [PLACE seokmun: A narrow place that looks like a way out, until it isn’t.]
[8] ¶ At Seokmun the Tang turn around. Out of the side valleys come the Mohe cavalry, into a Silla army that has not yet formed up. It is over in an afternoon.
[9] ¶ Wonsul sees the general ahead of him go down, and then the next one. He turns his horse toward the Mohe, which is the direction a son of Kim Yushin is supposed to turn.
[10] Wonsul: Let go.
[11] ¶ His aide, Danneung, has the bridle in both fists.
[12] Danneung: No. / Dying’s not the hard part, Lieutenant. Any fool can do it in the next ten breaths. / Picking where is hard. This is a ditch. Die here and you’ve bought nothing.
[13] Wonsul: My father— / Let go, or I’ll cut your hand off.
[14] Danneung: Then cut it. I’ll still be holding.
[15] ¶ He doesn’t cut it. Danneung turns the horse himself and runs it south through the dust, with a lieutenant on its back who screams at him the whole way. Seven Silla generals die in that valley. Wonsul is not one of them.
[16] [FORMATION Seokmun, eighth month, 672: Seven named commanders died at Seokmun. Silla stopped attacking after it, and spent three years building walls instead.]
[17] ── SCENE: The Apology ──
[18] ¶ Silla sends an apology to Chang’an and hands back the prisoners. Then it goes quiet, and starts building.
[19] ¶ The draft comes to the king’s table that winter. The court has read it. The court would like a word.
[20] ❝QUOTE (Samguk Sagi (三國史記) bk. 7, Silla Annals — King Munmu, yr. 12 (672), ninth month — memorial of apology to the Tang court) [King Munmu]: Your servant, guilty unto death, respectfully reports. … All the bamboo of the Southern Mountain would not be enough to write down your servant's crimes, nor all the forests of Baoxie to make his shackles. Flood our ancestral temple, tear your servant limb from limb: in this I await the imperial decision, and accept execution with a willing heart.❞
[21] True Bone minister: Majesty. “Tear your servant limb from limb”? We won the morning. / We are apologizing for the morning?
[22] King Munmu: We’re apologizing for the afternoon. / And for the next fortress. And the one after that.
[23] True Bone minister: …Who wrote this?
[24] King Munmu: My father. Thirteen years ago. / I’m only signing it.
[25] ¶ The minister thinks it is a joke. It is a room in Surabol, a year before Baekje fell, and a father asking his son a question.
[26] ▼ FLASHBACK 659 A room in Surabol, a year before Baekje falls
    [26.0] King Muyeol: Bupmin. What do you think happens after Baekje falls?
    [26.1] King Munmu: We move on Goryeo.
    [26.2] King Muyeol: And after that.
    [26.3] King Munmu: …Unification.
    [26.4] King Muyeol: No. / After that, **it is our turn**.
    [26.5] ¶ He lays it out the way another man would lay out a field. The Tang will not go home. They will put a governor in Sabi and call it a commandery. They will give you a title with the word _province_ in it and expect you to be flattered. They will keep your brother in Chang’an and call him a guest.
    [26.6] King Muyeol: When it comes, never strike first. / Wait until they have exhausted themselves in the north. / Take the fortresses back one at a time, and send an apology after each one. / What they want is not the land. It is the paperwork.
    [26.7] King Munmu: …And the sea?
    [26.8] King Muyeol: The sea is last. / After they have lost the horses.
    [26.9] King Munmu: Father. How do you know all of this?
    [26.10] King Muyeol: Li Shimin taught me. / I wrote down everything he intended to do to me.
[26] ▲ end flashback
[27] ¶ Munmu signs. The ink is still wet when the first stones of the new walls go in.
[28] ¶ **Wonsul came home alive. In his father’s house, that is the crime…!**

#92 Wonsul  (672 August)
Arc: Silla-Tang War · place: surabol · tone: family tragedy
Logline: Wonsul came home alive from Stone Gate. His father asks the king to execute him, and the king answers with something he said at fifteen.
=================================================================
[0] ¶ Wonsul gets home a day before the news does. It doesn’t help.
[1] ¶ His father’s gate stays shut. The lamp above it is his mother’s. **Lady Jiso** is King Muyeol’s daughter, and she keeps it lit every night her men are at war. Tonight it burns, and she does not come down.
[2] [MAP 672: ]
[3] ── SCENE: Father's House ──
[4] ¶ Inside, Yushin is told his son is at the gate. He doesn’t get up.
[5] Steward: My lord. It’s the young master. He’s hurt, I think. His horse is—
[6] Kim Yushin: He shamed the king’s command and the family name with it. He is not my son.
[7] ¶ The retreat is almost beside the point. A hundred men ran that afternoon and kept their fathers. But a house that came into Silla by treaty does not get to be ordinary, or it is simply Gaya again.
[8] Kim Yushin: Another man’s son may retreat. / Mine may not.
[9] ── SCENE: The King's Hall ──
[10] ¶ Yushin goes to the king and asks, in so many words, for his son to be put to death. It is the most formal request he has made in fifty years of service, and he makes it standing.
[11] King Munmu: Uncle. He was a lieutenant. Lieutenants follow. / If I execute every man who lived through Seokmun, I won’t have an army left to lose the next one with.
[12] Kim Yushin: The law is the law, Majesty. A Hwarang does not retreat.
[13] King Munmu: On your yard you once asked me which of the five I would break first. / I said retreat. I was fifteen. You didn’t ask my father to kill me.
[14] Kim Yushin: …You were not my son.
[15] ¶ The king has no answer to that. The old man knows it. Neither of them looks away first.
[16] Kim Yushin: Then do not execute him, Majesty. / But do not ask me to call him back into my house.
[17] King Munmu: …As you wish, Marshal.
[18] ── SCENE: The Hill Farms ──
[19] ¶ Wonsul does not go home. He goes into the hill farms east of the capital and works another man’s fields under no name at all, which is the one punishment his father did not think to ask for. He does not write. Twice he comes as far as the road below his father’s gate and turns back at the sight of his mother’s lamp.
[20] Farmer: You hold a hoe like it owes you money. / Soldier, were you?
[21] Wonsul: No. / …Not a good one.
[22] ¶ **Yushin is old now. The three sisters in the steam are not. They have kept his ledge warm for fifty years…!**

#93 Kim Yushin†  (673 July)
Arc: Silla-Tang War · place: surabol · tone: psychopomp elegy
Logline: Old now, Yushin still finds the cavern. The three in the steam look exactly the age they always looked.
=================================================================
[0] ══ DAY: THE LAKE REMEMBERS ══
[1] ¶ Old now, between campaigns that are mostly paperwork, Yushin still finds the cavern. The steam is thinner. The three are not. They look the same age they always looked — which is either mercy or mockery, and he has never asked which.
[2] ¶ Hyullé’s hand finds the water beside the ledge where he always sits, and stays there. Fifty years of the same ledge.
[3] Narim: You still undress like a soldier checking for wounds. / Sit. The counsel is shorter these days. So is the war. Slower. Let me look at you.
[4] Golhwa: He’s going to say it. / Watch — three, two —
[5] Kim Yushin: But Her Majesty is gone. / …I still hear myself saying it.
[6] Golhwa: Ugh… even in the Western Flower Field she gets the title. / What did that mortal have that we don’t? / …Don’t answer. Stay until the steam drops. Before the hill keeps you.
[7] Hyullé: I didn’t — bring — / …It’s just warmer there. / You always liked it. Come sit. Please.
[8] ¶ The steam thins. For a breath his father’s mouth is in the water — not the counsel, only the name — and then it is steam again.
[9] ¶ He sits. For once he does not rush the border. Narim talks about a tree that outlived three kings. Golhwa falls asleep against the stone mid-complaint. Hyullé says nothing, and that is the visit he will remember when the biographies start lying.
[10] ── SCENE: The Deathbed ──
[11] ¶ Seventh month, 673. He is seventy-nine. He has fought for sixty of those years and outlived nearly everyone worth outliving.
[12] ¶ The King comes to the house himself, which kings do not do. Munmu does it anyway — he has known this man his entire life, and for most of it has not been sure whether to call him _Marshal_ or _uncle_.
[13] ¶ The old man's eyes are already somewhere younger.
[14] King Munmu: Yushin…
[15] ¶ Nobody has called him by his bare name in forty-one years. The last one was a queen, on her coronation morning.
[16] Kim Yushin: Princess…
[17] Kim Yushin: …The boy. Is he eating?
[18] King Munmu: He’s farming. Badly. Shall I send for him?
[19] Kim Yushin: …No. / Good. That he’s eating.
[20] ❝QUOTE (Samguk Sagi (三國史記) bk. 43, Biographies — Kim Yushin (final counsel); Lee Byong-do ed., vol. 2, p. 404): I humbly pray Your Highness know that to succeed is not easy, and to keep what has been won is also hard. Keep petty men far and good men near.❞
[21] ¶ Kangrim reads his name three times at the bedside — Yushin. Yushin. Yushin. — before the marshal's last answer.
[22] Kangrim: Marshal. / One hundred and eight draws, one win that ended a friend, sixty years of being useful. / Question: were you becoming Silla — or proving you never needed their blood to outserve them?
[23] Kim Yushin: …I wanted in. / Wanting in is not shameful. Pretending I did not is.
[24] Kangrim: Clean answer. / His Majesty’s kingdom has room for men who told the truth late.
[25] ¶ When the escort walks out through the courtyard, Munhee is standing by the well. She is sixty-seven. She sees her brother walking beside the stranger. Nobody else in the yard does. Above the roof the eastern star is up, the one that sits among the stars without being one of them.
[26] Munhee: Brother. Are you a Silla man now?
[27] Kim Yushin: …I don’t know. Ask them for me.
[28] ¶ She lets him go without asking twice. There is nobody left now who calls her little sister.
[29] ¶ He is buried at Geumsan with the honours of a king and the rank of a subject. Somebody will close that gap. It takes a hundred and sixty years.
[30] ¶ — Kim Yushin —
[31] ¶ _His grandfather bought the family a rank with a kingdom. Everyone honoured the deal, and everyone remembered it. So he made himself the one thing they could not do without, and he was very, very good at it. He loved a queen for forty years and never once said so where it could be heard. They would not let him all the way in while he lived. Once he was safely dead, they made him a king._
[32] ── SCENE: Lady Jiso ──
[33] ¶ After the funeral Wonsul comes down from the hills at last and asks at the gate for his mother. The lamp is out. **Lady Jiso** has already cut her hair for the nunnery.
[34] Lady Jiso: A woman has three to follow. Her father, her husband, her son. / My husband would not call you son. How am I to be your mother?
[35] ¶ She does not come to the gate. The answer is carried out by a servant who cannot look at him. Wonsul stands in the road until dark and then goes back up into the hills. The record says only that he left weeping, and that he never stopped trying to give the afternoon back.
[36] ¶ **The king has buried his uncle. He still has one letter to answer, and a path nobody ever showed him…!**

=================================================================
#94 The Wanggeom's Guest  (673 Autumn)
Arc: Silla-Tang War · place: steam_cavern · tone: mythic coronation
Logline: The day after the funeral, Munmu signs a traitor’s death warrant, then finds his uncle’s spring. Something older than any kingdom is waiting on the water.
=================================================================
[0] ── SCENE: The Second Letter ──
[1] ¶ The day after the funeral, a letter falls out of a sleeve.
[2] ¶ It is short. It is addressed to the Tang garrison at Bear Ford, and it promises them a door in the wall of Surabol, the way a man at Daeya once promised Baekje a granary. The hand is very steady. The king knows that hand. It copied his letter to Xue Rengui.
[3] Daeto: Majesty. A softer word here and there—
[4] King Munmu: You said that in the writing room. / You copied my letter very well, Daeto. Copy this one.
[5] ¶ It is his own death warrant. Daeto copies it out fair, and his hand is still very steady. His wife and children are made slaves. Nobody mentions it at court.
[6] ── SCENE: The Steam Cavern ──
[7] ¶ That evening Munmu rides alone into the hills east of Surabol. His uncle never showed him the path. He finds it anyway, the way sons find what uncles hid on purpose.
[8] ¶ He strips at the rock lip as if obeying an order nobody ever gave him in writing, and steps into water so black it reflects nothing.
[9] ¶ Crimson leaves his shoulders the way a soldier sheds a campaign coat. Steam takes the rest. He does not look up until the water has him.
[10] ¶ For a long time he only stands in the water. He is forty-seven, and a king, and there is nobody left alive who taught him to ride. He lets the steam have his face, so that nobody has to see it. Not even the rock.
[11] ¶ They smell him before they see him. Uncle’s heat, father’s road-dust, both houses in one walk. He still thinks he is alone. Golhwa’s mouth opens and does not close. Hyullé cannot get a word out. Narim bites her lip and fails at being eldest.
[12] ¶ They know him. The **best of both**: they said it first when he was twenty-one and came in with a jar, and they say it again now that the uncle is ash. Gaya in the shoulders. Surabol in the mouth. Fire comes off Golhwa’s skin. Water streams from Hyullé’s chin. A leaf turns in the steam around Narim and will not fall.
[13] King Munmu: …You’re still here. / I brought a jar last time. I didn’t bring anything tonight.
[14] Narim: You brought him. On your shoulders. We can smell it. / Sit. Before you fall—
[15] ¶ He looks at her like she is kind. Narim cannot finish the sentence. She is out of breath, and pretends the steam did that. Uncle’s shoulders. Father’s mouth. She is not supposed to want both, tonight of all nights.
[16] Golhwa: He’s the one crying and I’m the one who can’t sit. / …Sorry. Ignore me. Stay till the steam drops.
[17] Hyullé: Hello. I’ll be quiet.
[18] ¶ That is all Hyullé gets out. She stands near him in the water and looks like she will break. He keeps the black water as a wall. He does not climb out.
[19] Narim: Sit down before you fall in again. / We are the mouths the hill uses. Wisdom, if you stand in the water and ask once. The uncle is gone. The hill is not.
[20] King Munmu: I came because he died. / …Will the west stay taken.
[21] ¶ Something goes out of the cave. When they speak again the eyes are solid: green, cyan, ember.
[22] Narim: The west will take your name and call it peace. / Keep a sea in the other hand.
[23] Golhwa: That was the hill. This is me. / Come back anyway. With nothing in your hands, like tonight. We like you better that way.
[24] ── SCENE: The Man on the Water ──
[25] ¶ Then the steam goes thin enough to see through, and a man stands on the water as if the lake were a court floor — old robes, sandalwood-coloured light, a face that has outlived every kingdom on the map. The three go still on the rock. This visitor is not theirs.
[26] Dangun: You wanted a king for all when you were six. / The title you are looking for is older than your father’s reforms. / Wanggeom — not Sacred Bone, not True Bone. The first who stayed when heaven descended.
[27] King Munmu: Who are you. / Which court sent you.
[28] Dangun: Asadal is dust. / The mandate is not. / Finish what your uncle could not name aloud.
[29] ¶ Munmu tells no one. The court records note only a day’s ride and a night’s silence. But he has heard the bear’s son’s name before, in his mother’s version, with extra garlic, and he keeps it.
[30] ¶ **Kim Punghun said he could wait for a ship. The ship is here…!**

=================================================================
#95 Maeso  (675 September)
Arc: Silla-Tang War · place: maeso · tone: grim war epic
Logline: Xue Rengui comes back by sea. His guide is a Silla boy whose father the king killed.
=================================================================
[0] ── SCENE: The Landing ──
[1] ¶ Xue Rengui comes back by sea in the ninth month. His pilot is Kim Punghun. Munmu killed his father. Now the son is showing the enemy fleet the way into his own coast.
[2] [MAP 675: Horses by sea, horses by land. Silla has decided this war is about horses.]
[3] ¶ He is older now. The white coat is a reputation he can no longer take off. Tang’s eastern command sits on his shoulders the way a yoke sits on an ox that still believes in the field. In a poor field at home, his ancestors are still waiting for their graves.
[4] ¶ Punghun stands at the bow beside him. He left Silla a boy, a hostage in the emperor’s guard. He is coming back as a guide.
[5] Xue Rengui: You know this coast, Master Kim.
[6] Kim Punghun: I know my father’s coast. / The king made it mine to sell.
[7] Xue Rengui: I am not buying anything. / I only ask where the sand is firm. For the horses.
[8] ¶ Punghun looks at the beach below Cheon Fortress for a long time.
[9] Kim Punghun: …There. Firm enough.
[10] Xue Rengui: Silla… the country that once fought beside us. / And now that country is to be my last opponent.
[11] ¶ He does not curse them. He checks the ji’s bindings, the same way he once checked plough-rope, and goes ashore.
[12] ¶ Above the beach at Cheon Fortress, a Silla general named **Munhun** lies flat in the dune grass and watches the boats come in. He has been told to stop the landing. He has decided to let it happen first.
[13] ¶ Beside him lies a ship captain named **Sideuk**, who has commanded boats for twelve years and never once won anything.
[14] Sideuk: General, they’re unloading the horses. Horses first.
[15] Munhun: Good. Let them.
[16] Sideuk: We were told to stop the landing.
[17] Munhun: We will. / A horse on wet sand can’t turn. Wait till the boats are empty.
[18] Sideuk: …Wet sand. I’ll remember that.
[19] ¶ When the last horse is off, Munhun stands up.
[20] Xue Rengui: To the boats.
[21] ¶ By evening Munhun has fourteen hundred heads, forty Tang ships, and a thousand horses standing in the surf with nobody to ride them. The sea road is closed again.
[22] ¶ Nobody ever learns whether Punghun knew about the sand. Xue does not ask him. He sends him back to Chang’an on the next empty transport, and neither country writes his name down again.
[23] ── SCENE: Maeso Fortress ──
[24] ¶ So the war moves inland, to a fortress on the Imjin where the road to Surabol begins.
[25] [PLACE maeso: Good walls. Terrible stables.]
[26] [FORMATION Maeso Fortress, twenty-ninth day of the ninth month, 675: 30,380 horses were taken, and weapons to match. Historians read the 200,000 as Silla counting generously; nobody argues about the horses.]
[27] ¶ The army at Maeso is mostly Mohe, and the Mohe are mostly horse. Thirty thousand of them graze the flats under the walls. The grass is outside. No fortress on that river was built to stable a herd.
[28] Silla commander: Forget the walls. / Cut the picket lines. Bring me the horses.
[29] ¶ The worst stretch of the line is under the walls, where the archers can see. A man nobody in the capital has seen for three years asks for it.
[30] Silla commander: Name?
[31] Wonsul: Lieutenant. Of Seokmun.
[32] ¶ Before dawn the herd moves all at once, and not toward the fortress.
[33] Mohe rider: The horses! The horses are going!
[34] ¶ Horses are the thing. An army that has lost thirty thousand horses on the Imjin is not riding to Surabol next spring, or the spring after.
[35] ¶ Afterwards the king sends for the lieutenant to give him rank. Wonsul comes in still smelling of horses.
[36] King Munmu: Your father would have—
[37] Wonsul: My father would have said I owe one afternoon, Majesty. I haven’t paid it yet.
[38] ── SCENE: The Fleet ──
[39] ¶ Out at sea off Cheon Fortress, Xue hears it from a courier: the army at Maeso has lost its horses.
[40] Xue Rengui: …So the horses are gone. / For a farmer, losing horses… is like losing the field.
[41] ¶ He withdraws without spectacle. The chronicle will remember Silla’s thirty thousand horses; it will remember less how quietly the White Tiger II accepted that the east was no longer his to harvest.
[42] ── SCENE: Surabol ──
[43] ¶ In Surabol the number arrives a day ahead of the generals.
[44] Messenger: Thirty thousand, three hundred and eighty, Majesty.
[45] King Munmu: …Heads?
[46] Messenger: Horses, Majesty.
[47] ¶ _After they have lost the horses._ Munmu is nearly fifty and still, occasionally, checking his father’s work against the day.
[48] ¶ The Tang history says Maeso was three Tang victories, after which Silla begged pardon. It does not mention the horses.
[49] King Munmu: Then get me ships. / It’s the sea now.
[50] ¶ **One last river mouth. One captain who has never won a fight. Three tries to end a war…!**

=================================================================
#96 Final Ford  (676 November)
Arc: Silla-Tang War · place: gibeolpo · tone: grim war epic — naval
Logline: At the river mouth where the Tang landed sixteen years ago, a captain who has never won anything loses twice on purpose. Xue Rengui watches his fleet sit down in the mud.
=================================================================
[0] ¶ In the second month, the emperor's headquarters quietly leaves Pyongyang. Then it moves further. Then nobody mentions it. Xue still has a fleet, and a fleet doesn't need a headquarters.
[1] [MAP 676: The protectorate packs for Liaodong. Xue Rengui keeps one fleet and one last idea.]
[2] ── SCENE: Final Ford ──
[3] ¶ The last of it happens at the mouth of the Geum, in the eleventh month. Sixteen years ago the Tang came in through this same water, onto a mile of grey mud, while Baekje watched from the high ground. Seongchung had begged a different king to hold it.
[4] ¶ The Silla ships belong to **Sideuk**, the captain who has never won anything. He takes them out on the ebb and loses.
[5] Silla helmsman: Sachan, we’re going out again?
[6] Sideuk: When the tide turns.
[7] ¶ He goes out again and loses again.
[8] Silla helmsman: …And a third time?
[9] Sideuk: Their ships are big. / A big ship can’t turn on the mudflats. Draw them in. / Like a horse on wet sand.
[10] ── SCENE: The Third Sortie ──
[11] ¶ The third time, Sideuk does not try to win. He runs.
[12] ¶ He takes eight boats up the estuary on the last of the flood, close enough to the Tang flagship to be insulting. Arrows thud into his deck. He lets them. Then he turns, badly, the way a beaten man turns, and makes for the mudflats.
[13] Silla helmsman: They’re coming! All of them— Sachan, the big ones are coming!
[14] Sideuk: Of course they are. They’ve beaten us twice. / Keep running. Look scared.
[15] Silla helmsman: I’m not pretending, sir.
[16] ¶ The tide turns under them. Sideuk’s boats float in a hand’s depth of water. The Tang tower-ships need a man’s height. One by one, the great hulls feel the mud take their keels, and stop, and lean.
[17] Sideuk: Now. Turn. Everyone, turn!
[18] ¶ What follows is twenty-two fights, large and small, in water too shallow for the ships that started them. Silla men cross the mud on planks, on oars, on their own bellies. The tower-ships cannot turn to face them. They can only lean further.
[19] ── SCENE: The Flagship ──
[20] ¶ On the flagship, Xue Rengui stands at the rail and watches his fleet sit down in the mud like oxen in a flooded field. He is sixty-two. He knows exactly what he is looking at. He grew up looking at it.
[21] Tang officer: Commander. We can still float the flagship on the night tide. The others—
[22] Xue Rengui: The others are a field we planted in the wrong season. / Float what floats. Take the men off the rest. Leave no one in the mud.
[23] ¶ He does not curse Silla. He never has. At midnight the flagship lifts off the mud, and he turns her west.
[24] Xue Rengui: Ancestors. / I asked you to wait a little longer. It was longer than I said. / I am coming home without the east. I still have the ji.
[25] ¶ No treaty comes after it, and no envoy. The Tang ships simply keep going west, and nobody on them looks back.
[26] [MAP 676: West. Nobody signs anything. The ships simply keep going.]
[27] ── SCENE: Surabol ──
[28] ¶ In Surabol the king waits a month for a letter from the west, so that he will at least have something to refuse. None comes.
[29] King Munmu: Have we… won…?
[30] Court scribe: Nobody has told us we haven’t, Majesty.
[31] ¶ He laughs, for the first time since the funeral, and goes to tell his mother.
[32] ¶ **The boy who stole a sentence at six is about to be king of all Samhan. His mother would like him to hold still…!**

=================================================================
#97 The King for All  (676)
Arc: Silla-Tang War · place: surabol · tone: hard-won resolution
Logline: On the morning he becomes king of all Samhan, Munmu opens the hall to the yard. Five summers later, Kangrim asks him the question.
=================================================================
[0] ¶ **Bupmin**, **King Munmu** now, stands where a six-year-old once stole a sentence. The war is won, the ally has been shown the door, and the childhood dream has had the bad manners to come true.
[1] [MAP 676: Sixteen years, start to finish. Watch where the blue stops.]
[2] ── SCENE: The Collar ──
[3] ¶ It ends where it began: a woman in a room, getting someone else ready.
[4] ¶ Munhee is seventy. She is the last person alive who remembers all of it from the inside, and she is straightening her son's collar. She was twenty-six when this story started. Her sister burned a skirt on a hill so that she could be married.
[5] Munhee: Hold still. Your collar is crooked.
[6] King Munmu: Mother. Today I become king of all Samhan.
[7] Munhee: Then all the more reason to hold still.
[8] King Munmu: Mother. / I kept the childhood sentence.
[9] Munhee: I know. / I packed for every country that tried to stop you.
[10] ¶ She has been in the room for every single one of them. The sword was never in her hand, and she is the only one still standing.
[11] Munhee: Your sister rode out of this room to Daeya. / Hold still. I’m not losing another one to a door.
[12] ¶ A letter has come from Chang’an. It is the first in Inmun’s hand in twenty years, and it is very short.
[13] Kim Inmun: Brother. / The emperor made me King of Silla for a season. I got as far as the coast road before he changed his mind. I am told I abdicated. I agreed. / Word came that you said my name. I heard it. / — Inmun
[14] Munhee: His handwriting hasn’t improved.
[15] ¶ She folds it into his sleeve, next to his arm, where he will feel it all day.
[16] King Munmu: Father used to say a thing. A kingdom that lasts a thousand years.
[17] Munhee: He always did round the numbers up.
[18] ¶ Silla lasts nine hundred and ninety-two years. He was, as usual, very slightly optimistic and essentially correct.
[19] ── SCENE: The Hall ──
[20] ¶ The hall is full of bone. True Bone in the front rows, Head-rank Six behind them, and behind them the new men nobody has a rank for yet: Baekje captains who fought for Silla, Goguryeo’s guest king and his officers, a Mohe interpreter. Out in the yard stand the ones with no bone at all. They have come to see what a king for all looks like. Mostly he looks tired.
[21] King Munmu: Open the doors. / All of them. The yard too.
[22] ¶ The doors open. The yard comes up to the threshold and stops there, the way people stop at a river.
[23] King Munmu: Sixteen years of war were paid for with grain borrowed from people who had none. / Every grain debt from the war years is cancelled. Today. / The men of Baekje and Goguryeo who bled under our banners will hold Silla ranks. The same ranks.
[24] True Bone elder: Majesty. The bone ranks are older than the throne. If a Baekje captain sits where—
[25] King Munmu: When I was six I said everyone would have to listen to me. Even the bone people. / …I meant you, my lord.
[26] ¶ Somebody in the yard laughs. Then the whole yard does. The elder sits down. It is the first time that hall has ever heard the yard.
[27] King Munmu: I asked my uncle once. Every kingdom, or every person who bleeds for one. He never answered. / Both. Write that down.
[28] ── SCENE: The Eastern Star ──
[29] ¶ Thirty-four winters ago, three men looked up at one star and wanted the same title. One died a guest in Chang’an, still calling himself a king. One died in his bed, and the king of the dead came to fetch him in person. One left the title in his son’s mouth.
[30] ¶ That night the son climbs the hill above Surabol where two boys once lay on their backs, arguing about the sky.
[31] King Munmu: Uncle always said it was a planet.
[32] ¶ It sits among the stars without being one of them. He looks at it until the cold gets into his knees. Then he walks down to his own house, like anybody.
[33] ── SCENE: The Ancestral Temple ──
[34] ¶ In the morning he reports to his father. The tablet stands in the ancestral temple, and beside it hangs the iron oath from Mount Gain, the one he swore over his uncle’s horse.
[35] King Munmu: Father. I broke it. Every line. / Baekje is ours. Its prince is in Luoyang, with a title and no country. / His sons are growing. I asked. The gods have been lenient with us both.
[36] ¶ He leaves the oath where it hangs. The kings of Silla will have to walk past it every time they visit their fathers. He wants them to read it.
[37] ── SCENE: Five Summers Later ──
[38] ¶ Five summers later the king for all is dying, and he has left instructions his ministers do not like. No mound in the hills beside his fathers. Burn him, and put what is left in the sea the Wa come across.
[39] King Munmu: The war is over. Melt the swords. Make ploughs. / Lighten the tax at the markets and the ferries. / And don’t build me a tomb. The people would only have to carry the stones.
[40] ¶ Kangrim reads his name three times at the bedside — Bupmin. Bupmin. Bupmin. — the name the boy stole a sentence with, not the one the ledger writes.
[41] Kangrim: King Munmu. / Sixteen years of war, one hill, one ally shown the door, and a yard you let into the hall. / One question, then we walk. Were you a king of Silla — or a king for all?
[42] King Munmu: …Ask the ones with no bone. / There are more of them.
[43] Kangrim: The ledger has never asked them anything. / …I suppose I’ll start. Come. The sea is this way.
[44] ❝QUOTE (Samguk Yusa (三國遺事) bk. 2, Wonder 2 — King Munmu becomes a dragon; Ha & Mintz tr., p. 95): After I am gone I wish to become a great dragon that guards the country, to uphold the Buddha’s law and protect the realm.❞
[45] ¶ They burn him on the shore and put his bones under a rock a hundred paces out to sea, which is still there, and is the only royal tomb in the world with tides.
[46] ── SCENE: The Tablet ──
[47] ¶ Eleven years after the tide closes over him, an envoy comes from the Empress’s court with a complaint that is thirty years late. King Muyeol’s tablet in Silla’s ancestral temple says Taejong, and Taejong is the Second Emperor’s temple name, and a vassal may not share a name with the Son of Heaven. Nobody from the Empress’s court mentions the iron oath hanging beside the tablet, broken in every line.
[48] Tang envoy: Your late king has borrowed a name that belongs to the Second Emperor. / Change it.
[49] ¶ Munmu’s son answers in writing.
[50] Silla reply: Our late king had a great deal of virtue. While he lived he had a good minister, Kim Yushin, and the two of them were of one mind, and they made the three Han one. / We thought that was worth a name. We did not know it was already taken.
[51] ¶ The court reads the name Kim Yushin, and an old archivist goes looking. He finds a note in the late emperor’s own hand, from his boyhood: a voice in the sky once told him that one of the Thirty-Three Heavens had been born in the east as a general. Nobody ever learned whose voice it was. Heaven gossips more than it lets on. The complaint is dropped. The tablet still says Taejong.
[52] ¶ **But we left someone in the snow. The winter Pyongyang fell, a Mohe father walked north with something in his pack…!**

=================================================================
#98 Balhae  (698)
Arc: Epilogue · place: jolbon · tone: new-dawn coda
Logline: The winter after Pyongyang falls, an old man carries a piece of a crown through the snow.
=================================================================
[0] ¶ The winter after Pyongyang falls, the mountains of Manchuria do not care who won. Snow comes to the knee, then to the thigh, and the wind off the ridges finds every seam a coat has. **Gulgul** walks in front, bent under a leather pack and wrapped in so much fur he looks like something the forest would hunt. His son walks in his tracks, because there are no other tracks.
[1] [MAP 720: The north, after Goguryeo.]
[2] ¶ In the pack, under dried millet and a spare pair of boots, wrapped in a strip of red silk, rides a piece of the Goguryeo crown no longer than a finger: one gold branch snapped off when the palace fell, its little leaves still hanging on their wires. Nobody else would carry it north. Behind them is the smoke of someone else’s victory. Ahead is only the cold that Yeon once pulled a Mohe boy out of.
[3] [CARD Dae Joyoung: Dae Joyoung. A boy with frozen feet, and a piece of a crown in the pack.]
[4] Dae Joyoung: Father… / Father, my feet… I can’t feel my feet.
[5] Gulgul: Good. / Better than feeling them.
[6] Dae Joyoung: What kind of— Father!
[7] Gulgul: There. Under the rock. / A little more.
[8] ── SCENE: The Cave ──
[9] ¶ The cave is a crack in the mountain’s side, deep enough to put the wind behind them. Gulgul strikes the flint four times before the moss takes. The fire is the size of two cupped hands. He sets the pack down beside it, and the boy, thawing, sees a small gold shine through a split seam in the leather, brighter than a fire that size has any right to make it.
[10] Dae Joyoung: Father. What’s… that? / The shiny thing. That. / Is that gold? We had gold? Then why is it always millet gruel—
[11] Gulgul: Keep your voice down.
[12] ¶ Gulgul looks at the cave mouth for a long time, as if the snow might be listening. Then he pulls the red silk free. On his palm lies the gold branch, bent where it was torn, its leaves trembling in the heat off the fire.
[13] Gulgul: A piece of the crown. / The Goguryeo crown.
[14] Dae Joyoung: …Did you steal it?
[15] Gulgul: I took it. / Nobody else was going to.
[16] Dae Joyoung: But why you? / You’re… Mohe. Everybody says so.
[17] Gulgul: …Yes. I’m Mohe.
[18] ¶ Gulgul is not a man who tells stories. He tells this one the way he would report a border skirmish: in order, without adjectives, looking at the fire instead of the boy.
[19] Gulgul: I was younger than you. Our village burned. / Goguryeo soldiers came through. General Yeon’s men. / I stood in the doorway. A doorway with no roof over it.
[20] Dae Joyoung: …Why?
[21] Gulgul: Don’t know. / It was our house.
[22] ▼ FLASHBACK 634 A Mohe doorway, thirty-four winters before
    [22.0] ¶ A doorway with no house behind it. Snow on the ash. A Mohe boy holds a stick the way he has seen men hold spears. A big man in red-edged armor gets down off a red-bay horse, walks up until the stick touches his chest, laughs, and pulls off his gloves.
    [22.1] Yeon Gesomun: Look at this one. Guarding a house that’s already burned. / Good. Get on.
    [22.2] ¶ Years later, on the north wall of Pyongyang in a winter worse than this one, the same man stands with the grown boy a step behind him and the river frozen white below. He says the thing he says every winter, to anyone in earshot, as if the cold might forget it otherwise.
    [22.3] Yeon Gesomun: Cold?
    [22.4] Gulgul: …No, sir.
    [22.5] Yeon Gesomun: Liar. I’m cold too. / Remember it anyway. Kings die, courts get tired, walls come down— / **Goguryeo never dies.**
[22] ▲ end flashback
[23] ¶ The fire has sunk to coals. Gulgul turns the gold over once in his fingers.
[24] Gulgul: I don’t know how many times he said it. / Every winter. Drunk or sober. Before a fight, after one.
[25] ¶ He wraps the silk around the branch again and puts it in the boy’s hands.
[26] Gulgul: Keep it under the coat. / By the Holy King’s bow — if they see gold, they will remember we were a country.
[27] Dae Joyoung: Father — / When we stop… what do we call it?
[28] Gulgul: He called it Goguryeo. / Everyone else got tired and said Goryeo. / You — you say it the way he would have wanted.
[29] ¶ The boy holds the bundle to the coals. It is warm already, from the pack, from his father’s back. Outside, the snow keeps filling the cave mouth. He presses the cloth once, gold against his palm, and answers the empty north the only way the chronicle will keep.
[30] Dae Joyoung: Goguryeo never dies…!
[31] ¶ The last coal goes out. Cut to black.
[32] ── SCENE: Thirty Winters On ──
[33] ¶ They walk on. Thirty years later, in 698, the boy will raise a kingdom called Balhae on those three words, and the shard will still be warm.
[34] ¶ His capital will be a stamped grid of halls on the Mudanjiang. Lotus tiles. A stone lantern. Nobody there will need telling what the old country was called.
[35] ¶ So this story ends with two kings under one sky, each sure the sky meant him. In the south, a dead king lies under a rock in the sea, listening for the ones with no bone. In the north, a boy with frozen feet carries a piece of a crown. From high enough up, you can’t tell which of them is the King for All. The sky stopped trying a long time ago. It just watches the boy.
[36] ¶ Dae Joyoung keeps walking north, one hand on the gold under his coat.
[37] ¶ THE END
